sub_strands.sub_strand: Conversational Skills: Polite Language (Theme 1: Personal responsibility)
learning_experiences: make a list of necessary details about people that one needs to know for effective introduction,
brainstorm different types of introduction,
list polite expressions that can be used during the introduction,
match polite expressions to corresponding types of introduction,
discuss reasons for using polite language in introductions,
use games such as ‘catch the ball’ for the introduction of others,
role-play different contexts of self-introduction with peers,
review an audio or video recording of formal and informal introductions.
key_inquiry_questions: Why is it important for people to introduce themselves?
sub_strands.core_competences: Communication: It is developed as the learner listens critically and speaks clearly and effectively during role play of self-introduction with peers.
sub_strands.values: Respect is developed as learners acknowledge diverse opinions while brainstorming different types of introduction with peers.
sub_strands.pcis:
Peace education is enhanced as the learner uses games such as ‘catch the ball” for the introduction of others.
Effective communication is enhanced as the learner uses polite language during introductions.
sub_strands.links: The learner is able to use the concept of polite language while working with peers in various subjects such as Religious Education.

outcomes.text: identify polite expressions used in the introduction of self and others
use polite expressions in the introduction of self and others in different speaking contexts
model respectful behaviour during introductions

skills.name: Use polite expressions to introduce yourself and others
skills.mastery: Chooses the polite way to introduce yourself, a friend or a visitor (May I introduce my friend, Wanjiru? Pleased to meet you), puts the person of honour first, and spots a rude or blunt turn, in 8 of 10 new items.

prerequisites.reason: Grade 6 English taught it first. Proposed, to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

misconceptions.error: Introduces a person bluntly (This is Wanjiru. Shake.).

example.question: Which is the polite way to introduce your friend to the headteacher.
example.wrong_answer: This is my friend. He is Juma.
example.correct_answer: Madam, may I introduce my friend, Juma?

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "This is my friend. He is Juma." next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: A polite introduction asks permission and uses a title.
misconceptions.feedback: A polite introduction uses words such as may I introduce and a title for an older person: Madam, may I introduce my friend, Juma?
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Introduces the older or senior person to the younger one, not the other way round.

example.question: Whom do you name first when introducing your friend to the headteacher.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "your friend" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: The person of higher rank is named first.
misconceptions.feedback: We introduce the younger or less senior person to the older or senior one: name the headteacher first, then your friend.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Replies with no polite words after an introduction (Okay.).

example.question: You are introduced to a visitor. Which reply is polite.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Okay." next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Greet and show you are glad to meet the person.
misconceptions.feedback: A polite reply to an introduction is Pleased to meet you or How do you do.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Introduces self without a name or with a rude opening (Me, I am Otieno).

example.question: Which is the best way to introduce yourself at a new school.
example.correct_answer: Good morning. My name is Otieno, and I am in Grade 7.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Me, I am Otieno." next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Greet, give your name and one useful detail.
misconceptions.feedback: To introduce yourself, greet the person, say your name and add one useful detail: Good morning. My name is Otieno, and I am in Grade 7.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

sub_strands.sub_strand: Extensive Reading: Independent Reading (Theme 1: Personal responsibility)
learning_experiences: think-pair-share on the factors to consider when selecting reading material,
select appropriate reading materials related to personal responsibility,
set and share reading goals for the session,
read selected print and non-print materials independently,
observe good reading habits,
keep a portfolio or a journal of their experiences during the reading session,
conduct peer review of the portfolios and journals kept.
key_inquiry_questions: How can you ensure that you benefit from a reading session?
sub_strands.core_competences: Critical Thinking and Problem Solving is developed as the learner searches, collects, processes, and uses information from selected texts.
sub_strands.values:
Respect is developed as learners avoid distracting others by observing good reading habits.
Responsibility is nurtured as the learner is guided in selecting material that they consider appropriate for self and as they track personal progress.
sub_strands.pcis: Effective Communication is enhanced as learner shares their experiences during the think-pair-share activity with peers.
sub_strands.links: The learner uses the concept of independent reading in many subjects such as Agriculture.

outcomes.text: identify a variety of texts for independent reading
read selected materials for information and enjoyment
appreciate the value of independent reading in lifelong learning

skills.name: Choose a text that suits a purpose: fiction, non-fiction and independent reading
skills.mastery: Chooses the book or text that fits what the reader needs (information, enjoyment, a topic, a level), tells fiction from non-fiction, and does not choose by the cover, the length or the title alone, in 8 of 10 new items.
question_forms: choose the book for a purpose
judge the relevance of a text

prerequisites.reason: Grade 6 English taught it first. Proposed, to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.
Grade 6 English taught it first. Proposed, to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

misconceptions.error: Chooses a book by its cover or its length alone.

example.question: You need facts about Kenyan birds. Which book do you choose.
example.wrong_answer: the book with the nicest cover
example.correct_answer: a book called A Guide to the Birds of Kenya

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "the book with the nicest cover" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Choose by the topic and purpose, not the picture.
misconceptions.feedback: Choose a text by what you need: the title, the contents and the topic show whether it fits.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Mixes up fiction and non-fiction.

example.question: Which is a non-fiction text.
example.wrong_answer: a story about a talking hare
example.correct_answer: a book about how rain forms

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "a story about a talking hare" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Non-fiction gives facts about real things.
misconceptions.feedback: Fiction is made up (stories). Non-fiction gives facts about real things (an encyclopedia, a news report).
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Chooses a book that is too hard or too easy for the reader.

example.question: Which book suits a Grade 7 learner reading for fun on a weekend.
example.wrong_answer: a picture book for a Grade 1 child
example.correct_answer: a short adventure novel for young teenagers

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "a picture book for a Grade 1 child" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: A book should suit the reader's age and interest.
misconceptions.feedback: A suitable text matches the reader's age, level and interest.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Does not match the text to the purpose (a story for information).

example.question: You want to find out how a pump works. Which is the best text.
example.correct_answer: an illustrated science book on pumps

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "a poem about water" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Information is found in non-fiction.
misconceptions.feedback: To find information choose a non-fiction text on the topic. Stories and poems are mainly for enjoyment.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

sub_strands.sub_strand: Word Classes: Nouns (Theme 1: Personal responsibility)
learning_experiences: read a print or non-print text,
identify common, proper, concrete, and abstract nouns,
work with peers to search online for examples of the common, proper, concrete, and abstract nouns, and compile a list of the nouns,
listen to a poem or a story and categorise the nouns used,
mention examples of common, proper, concrete and abstract nouns in the classroom and school,
construct sentences using common, proper, concrete, and abstract nouns,
complete substitution tables with the different types of nouns,
engage in language games such as scrabble, puzzles, code words, and guessing games,
write and display stories, songs, or poems featuring the different types of nouns.
key_inquiry_questions: Why is it important to identify items by name?
sub_strands.core_competences: Learning to Learn: It is enhanced as the learner is motivated to learn continuously and work collaboratively while engaging in language games such as scrabble, puzzles, code words, and guessing games on nouns.
sub_strands.values:
Unity is fostered as the learner engages in games with peers and searches online for examples of concrete, proper and common nouns.
Patriotism is promoted as learners identify with their locality as they talk about people, places, and institutions in their community.
sub_strands.pcis: Digital Citizenship and Cyber wellness is enhanced as the learner searches online for examples of common, proper and concrete nouns.
sub_strands.links: The learner uses the concept of nouns in learning other languages such as Kiswahili.

outcomes.text: identify the different types of nouns from a print or digital text
use different types of nouns in sentences
appreciate the role of correct grammar in written and spoken communication

skills.name: Tell common, proper, collective and abstract nouns apart
skills.mastery: Names a noun as common (river), proper (Mombasa), collective (a flock of birds) or abstract (courage), picks the collective noun that goes with a group (a swarm of bees), and writes a capital letter for a proper noun only, in 8 of 10 new items.

prerequisites.reason: Grade 6 English taught it first. Proposed, to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.
Grade 5 English taught it first. Proposed, to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

leads_to.reason: Grade 8 English builds on this skill. Proposed, to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

misconceptions.error: Writes a proper noun with a small letter (kisumu, december) or a common noun with a capital.

example.question: We go to ___ every December.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "kisumu" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Names of particular places, people, days and months start with a capital letter.
misconceptions.feedback: A proper noun names one particular person, place or month, so it starts with a capital letter: Kisumu, Wanjiru, December.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Uses the wrong collective noun for a group (a herd of birds, a swarm of cattle).

example.question: A ___ of bees settled on the tree.

misconceptions.cause: Uses one word, such as group, or the word learnt first, for every group.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "herd" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Each group has its own word: a swarm of bees, a flock of birds, a herd of cattle.
misconceptions.feedback: Each kind of group has its own collective noun: a swarm of bees, a flock of birds, a herd of cattle, a pride of lions.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Thinks a collective noun is always plural (the team are winning, a flocks of birds).

example.question: A ___ of birds flew over the school.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "flocks" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: A collective noun names one group, so a flock is one thing.
misconceptions.feedback: A collective noun is one word for a whole group, so we write a flock of birds, not a flocks of birds.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Calls an idea or feeling a common noun for things we can touch, or the other way round.

example.question: Which noun is abstract: bridge, courage, bottle, drum.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "bridge" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Ask: can I touch or see it? Courage is an idea.
misconceptions.feedback: An abstract noun names an idea or a feeling, such as courage, joy or freedom. A common noun for a thing, such as a bridge, can be seen or touched.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Calls a name of a kind (river, city) a proper noun, or a particular name a common noun.

example.question: Which is a proper noun: city, Nairobi, river, teacher.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "city" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: A proper noun is the name of one particular place or person.
misconceptions.feedback: Nairobi is the name of one particular city, so it is a proper noun. City is the word for every city, so it is a common noun.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Takes one member of the group, or the person who looks after it, for the collective noun.

example.question: Which noun is a collective noun.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "player" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: A collective noun names the whole group as one.
misconceptions.feedback: A collective noun is one word for a whole group (team, herd, class, family). A player or a farmer is one member or one person.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

sub_strands.sub_strand: Intensive Reading: Trickster Narratives (Theme 1: Personal responsibility)
learning_experiences: engage in pre-reading activities such as previewing the title of the narrative, using picture clues, and brainstorming,
recount the events in the trickster narrative and highlight the trick in the narrative,
discuss the various character traits displayed by the characters,
brainstorm on the moral lessons from the narrative,
work collaboratively to retell a trickster narrative,
relate characters and events in the trickster narrative to real-life situations,
collaborate with peers to explore and share how personal responsibility can be derived from the narrative’s moral lessons.
key_inquiry_questions: Why would we listen to trickster narratives?
sub_strands.core_competences: Creativity and imagination: It is enhanced as the learner undertakes the task of retelling a trickster narrative.
sub_strands.values: Integrity is enhanced as learner relates the moral in the trickster narrative to real-life situations.
sub_strands.pcis: Effective communication is enhanced as the learner retells trickster narratives.
sub_strands.links: The learner is able to relate the concept of moral lessons to other learning areas such as Social Studies.

outcomes.text: identify the main events in trickster narratives
analyse the characters in narratives
appreciate the importance of trickster narratives in the inculcation of values

skills.name: Know trickster narratives and the lessons they teach
skills.mastery: Says that a trickster is a clever character who gets what it wants by a trick (Hare, Spider), names the trick and who is fooled, and says what the story teaches, and does not call the trickster a hero or the fooled one a trickster, in 8 of 10 new items.
question_forms: choose the trick or the lesson
choose what the trickster is like

prerequisites.reason: Grade 6 English taught it first. Proposed, to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

misconceptions.error: Calls the trickster a hero or the fooled character the trickster.

example.question: In many stories Hare fools Lion. Who is the trickster.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Lion" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: The trickster is the one who plays the trick.
misconceptions.feedback: The trickster is the clever character who gets what it wants by a trick. The one who is fooled is not the trickster.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Thinks a trickster wins by being strong.

example.question: How does a trickster usually win.
example.correct_answer: by being clever and using a trick

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "by being the strongest" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Tricksters use their wits.
misconceptions.feedback: A trickster wins by cleverness and tricks, not by strength.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Takes the wrong lesson from a trickster story (it is good to cheat).

example.question: A greedy character is tricked and loses his food. What does the story teach.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Cheating is always good." next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: The lesson is usually about the fooled character's fault.
misconceptions.feedback: Trickster stories often teach a lesson about greed, pride or foolishness. They do not teach that cheating is good.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Describes a trickster as honest and slow.

example.question: Which words describe a trickster.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "honest and slow" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: A trickster is quick-witted.
misconceptions.feedback: A trickster is clever, quick and cunning, and often a small or weak animal.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

sub_strands.sub_strand: Handwriting: Legibility and Neatness (Theme 1: Personal responsibility)
learning_experiences: listen to an audio clip on the importance of developing legible and neat handwriting,
study written samples of legible and neat handwriting featuring all letters of the alphabet and short texts,
discuss the features of legible and neat handwriting, including shaping letters, joining and spacing letters and words,
practise handwriting games such as blind writing, speed writing, and letter stations,
suggest ways of correcting bad handwriting habits such as joining letters and words inappropriately,
copy given texts on the theme of personal responsibility on charts and display for peer evaluation and correction,
write short paragraphs legibly and neatly, and share with peers for peer review.
key_inquiry_questions: Why should we write legibly and clearly?
sub_strands.core_competences: Learning to Learn: It is developed as the learner collaborates with peers to suggest ways of correcting bad handwriting habits.
sub_strands.values:
Respect is achieved as learners copy given texts on the theme of personal responsibility and display on charts for peer evaluation and correction.
Social justice is enhanced as the learner fosters non-discrimination while reviewing each other’s written work.
sub_strands.pcis: Effective communication is developed as the learner writes short paragraphs legibly and shares with peers.
sub_strands.links: The learner relates the concept of legible and neat handwriting to their learning in Kiswahili.

outcomes.text: describe features of legible and neat handwriting for efficient writing
write texts legibly and neatly for effective communication
acknowledge the importance of writing neatly and legibly

skills.name: Describe the features of legible and neat handwriting
skills.mastery: Names the features of neat handwriting (letters of an even size that sit on the line, tall and short letters kept distinct, clear spaces between words, a steady slant) and says why it matters, and does not take fast, decorated or crowded writing for neat, in 8 of 10 new items.

leads_to.reason: Grade 8 English builds on this skill. Proposed, to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

misconceptions.error: Thinks letters of different sizes, or letters that float above the line, are fine.

example.question: Which is a feature of neat handwriting.
example.correct_answer: letters of an even size on the line

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "letters of different sizes" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Look at the size and the line.
misconceptions.feedback: Neat handwriting has letters of an even size that sit on the line. Tall letters (b, d, h, l) are taller and short letters (a, c, e, o) are shorter, in the same way each time.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Leaves no clear spaces between words.

example.question: What should there be between words in neat handwriting.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "no space" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: A reader needs to see where one word ends.
misconceptions.feedback: There is a clear space between words so that the reader can see where each word starts and ends.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Thinks writing quickly or pressing hard is the way to neat writing.

example.question: What should Peter work on to make his handwriting easier to read.
example.correct_answer: keep the letters even and leave spaces between words

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "write faster" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Neat writing is steady, not rushed.
misconceptions.feedback: Writing fast or pressing hard does not make handwriting neat. Even letters and clear spaces do.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Thinks loops, decoration or colour make handwriting better.

example.question: Which handwriting is easiest to read.
example.correct_answer: plain, even letters on the line

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "letters with loops and decorations" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Plain letters are easiest to read.
misconceptions.feedback: Legible handwriting is plain and clear. Decorations and unusual shapes make it harder to read.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

sub_strands.sub_strand: Oral Presentations: Oral Narratives (Theme 2: Science and health education)
learning_experiences: watch live or recorded oral performances of narratives as a class,
search online or offline for information on performance techniques, in pairs, and make presentations to peers,
discuss the oral performance techniques,
perform oral narratives while peers watch, record, and then give feedback,
compose oral narratives and suggest to peers the most suitable ways of performing them.
key_inquiry_questions: What makes one a good storyteller?
sub_strands.core_competences: Creativity and Imagination: It is developed as learner undertakes tasks such as creating and retelling narratives, which require remembering scenarios.
sub_strands.values: Patriotism is achieved as learners compose and perform narratives on national values.
sub_strands.pcis: Environmental conservation is enhanced as learner performs narratives on the need to take care of the environment.
sub_strands.links: The skill of making presentations relates to showcasing of presentations in Creative Arts and Sports.

outcomes.text: outline the oral narrative performance techniques for effective delivery
use oral narrative techniques during the performance
appreciate the importance of performance techniques in the successful delivery of oral material

skills.name: Know the techniques of telling an oral narrative
skills.mastery: Names how a good storyteller uses the voice (loud and soft, fast and slow), pauses, gestures, face, eye contact and audience participation, and picks the technique that fits a part of a story, in 8 of 10 new items.
question_forms: choose the best way to tell this part

misconceptions.error: Thinks a good storyteller keeps the same voice throughout.

example.question: Which helps a storyteller most when the lion roars.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "a flat, even voice" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: The voice should fit the character.
misconceptions.feedback: A storyteller changes the voice to suit each character and event: loud for a roar, soft for a secret.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Races through the exciting part with no pause.

example.question: What should a storyteller do just before the surprise.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "speak faster" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: A pause builds suspense.
misconceptions.feedback: A short pause before a surprise makes the listeners wait and wonder.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Looks at the floor or the ceiling while telling a story.

example.question: Where should a storyteller look.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "at the floor" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Eye contact keeps the audience with you.
misconceptions.feedback: A storyteller looks at the listeners to keep their attention and to show that the story is for them.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Does not let the audience join in a song or a repeated line.

example.question: Which technique brings the audience into the story.
example.correct_answer: asking them to repeat the chorus

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "reading from a paper" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: A call and answer makes the audience part of the story.
misconceptions.feedback: In an oral narrative the audience may join in a song or a repeated line. This is called audience participation.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Thinks gestures and facial expression are not needed.

example.question: How can a storyteller show that a character is afraid.
example.correct_answer: step back and make a scared face

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "stand still with no expression" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: A face and body show feelings.
misconceptions.feedback: Gestures and facial expressions show feelings and actions: a scared face, a step back, hands up.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

sub_strands.sub_strand: Intensive reading: Simple poems (Theme 2: Science and health education)
learning_experiences: listen and respond to live or recorded poetry recitation,
discuss what makes reading simple poems interesting,
pick out poems from a variety of texts and read them out aloud,
recite poems that address science and health issues such as HIV and AIDS,
provide feedback to peers and seek help where necessary.
key_inquiry_questions: How are poems different from other forms of literary genres?
sub_strands.core_competences: Self-efficacy: It is enhanced as learners recite poems on HIV and AIDS with confidence.
sub_strands.values:
Peace is enhanced as learners work in teams during the poetry recitation.
Social justice is developed as learners recite poems that promote fairness in society.
sub_strands.pcis: Health education is promoted as learners recite poems that address health issues such as HIV and AIDS.
sub_strands.links: The learner relates the skills of recitation to performance techniques in other learning areas such as Creative Arts and Sports.

outcomes.text: distinguish between poems and other literary genres
recite a variety of simple poems for enjoyment
collaborate in poetry recitation for enjoyment and learning

sub_strands.sub_strand: Word Classes: Nouns (Theme 2: Science and health education)
learning_experiences: search for examples of count, non-count, singular, and plural nouns from the internet, write them and post them on the class reading wall,
listen to an audio text on the theme of science and health education, and pick out the target nouns,
pick out count, non-count, singular, and plural nouns from newspapers and magazine articles,
identify objects in the classroom and categorise them as count or non-count nouns,
change singular nouns to plural and vice versa,
construct sentences using the specified types of nouns orally and in writing,
work with peers to complete crossword puzzles with the target nouns,
work with peers to create posters using the learnt nouns, and post them on the class reading wall or share using digital learning platforms.
key_inquiry_questions: How can you group things that cannot be counted?
sub_strands.core_competences: Collaboration: It is achieved as the learner creates posters and poems, and shares them on the classroom wall or through digital learning platforms. This enhances teamwork among the learners.
sub_strands.values:
Unity is enhanced as learners work together to identify the different types of nouns in the classroom.
Respect is achieved as learners take turns to work with peers to create posters using the learnt nouns.
sub_strands.pcis:
Effective communication is achieved as the learner uses nouns in varied contexts correctly.
Health Education is promoted as the learner listens to an audio text on health issues.
sub_strands.links: The learner relates the concept of count and non-count nouns to their learning of nouns in Kiswahili.

outcomes.text: identify count, non-count, singular, and plural nouns from a variety of texts
use count, non-count, singular, and plural nouns in sentences
appreciate the importance of the correct use of nouns in communication

skills.name: Use count and non-count nouns: many, much, a few, a little
skills.mastery: Tells a count noun (chair, chairs) from a non-count noun (water, advice), uses many and a few with count nouns and much and a little with non-count nouns, and does not write advices, informations or furnitures, in 8 of 10 new items.

prerequisites.reason: Grade 6 English taught it first. Proposed, to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.
Grade 6 English taught it first. Proposed, to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

skills.name: Form singular and plural nouns correctly
skills.mastery: Writes the plural of nouns with the usual -s or -es, -ies after a consonant and y (baby, babies), -ves (knife, knives), the irregular plurals (child, children; man, men; tooth, teeth) and the nouns that do not change (sheep), in 8 of 10 new items.

prerequisites.reason: Grade 5 English taught it first. Proposed, to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

misconceptions.error: Uses much with a count noun or many with a non-count noun.

example.question: There were too ___ people at the gate.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "much" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: People can be counted, so many. Water cannot, so much.
misconceptions.feedback: Use many with nouns we can count (many people) and much with nouns we cannot count (much water).
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Adds -s to a non-count noun (advices, informations, furnitures, equipments, luggages).

example.question: She gave me some good ___.

misconceptions.cause: Many of these words have a plural form in Kiswahili or in the mother tongue.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "advices" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Advice is one thing that is not counted: some advice, a piece of advice.
misconceptions.feedback: Advice, information, furniture, luggage and equipment are not counted, so they have no plural form. Say some advice or a piece of advice.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Uses a few with a non-count noun or a little with a count noun.

example.question: Add a ___ sugar to the tea.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "few" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Sugar cannot be counted, so a little. Mangoes can, so a few.
misconceptions.feedback: A few goes with nouns we count (a few mangoes). A little goes with nouns we cannot count (a little sugar).
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Puts a or an before a non-count noun (a rice, an advice).

example.question: Mama bought ___ rice at the market.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "a rice" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Rice is not counted one by one, so use some, not a.
misconceptions.feedback: A and an are for one thing that can be counted. For rice, water or milk say some rice or a bag of rice.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Adds -s to an irregular noun (childs, mans, tooths, foots, mouses).

example.question: The ___ are playing football.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "childs" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Some nouns change inside or have their own plural: child, children.
misconceptions.feedback: Some plurals are irregular and must be learnt: child, children; man, men; woman, women; tooth, teeth; foot, feet.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Adds -s after a consonant and y (babys, storys, countrys).

example.question: The nurse looked after three ___.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "babys" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: After a consonant, y changes to ies: baby, babies.
misconceptions.feedback: When a noun ends in a consonant and y, change the y to ies: baby, babies; story, stories; country, countries.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Adds -s to nouns that change f or fe to ves (knifes, leafs, wolfs, lifes).

example.question: We cut the meat with two sharp ___.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "knifes" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Say the plural aloud: knives has a v sound.
misconceptions.feedback: Some nouns that end in f or fe change to -ves in the plural: knife, knives; leaf, leaves; wolf, wolves; life, lives.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Adds -s to a noun that stays the same in the plural (sheeps, fishs, deers).

example.question: Our uncle keeps twenty ___ in the village.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "sheeps" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Sheep, deer and fish do not change in the plural.
misconceptions.feedback: Some nouns have the same form in the singular and the plural: one sheep, ten sheep; one deer, two deer.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Adds only -s after s, x, ch, sh (boxs, buss, churchs, dishs).

example.question: Mother washed all the ___.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "dishs" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: After sh, ch, s and x add -es so that the ending can be said.
misconceptions.feedback: Nouns that end in s, x, ch or sh add -es in the plural: box, boxes; bus, buses; church, churches; dish, dishes.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Calls a noun that cannot be counted a count noun, or one that can be counted a non-count noun.

example.question: Which noun is a non-count noun.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "chair" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Ask: can I say one, two, three of it?
misconceptions.feedback: A count noun can have a number before it (three chairs). A non-count noun cannot (water, milk, rice, advice).
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Cannot tell the singular from the plural of an irregular noun (thinks children is singular, or that mouse is plural).

example.question: Which word is a plural noun.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "child" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Plural means more than one.
misconceptions.feedback: Children, men, women, teeth and feet are plural nouns with irregular forms. Child, man, woman, tooth and foot are singular.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

sub_strands.sub_strand: Intensive Reading: Class Reader (Theme 2: Science and health education)
learning_experiences: study the cover page of a class reader, read the blurb and highlight the outstanding features,
discuss the title of the class reader,
research online for more information about the author and the setting of the story,
make oral presentations to the class on their findings from the research,
identify words, images, and details that describe the setting in terms of place and time,

design a graphic organiser such as a mind map or tree map to identify the setting, share and give feedback using summary charts such as what I know - where I learned it - what I want to know - what I learned (K-W-W-L) chart to visualise what has been learned,
make short notes on the setting and the author.
key_inquiry_questions: Why should we not judge a book by its cover?
sub_strands.core_competences:
Learning to Learn: It is enhanced as learners build on their learning experiences through analysis of the setting and research on the author.
Critical thinking is developed as learners explore the links between different events through tasks like creating graphic organisers that cultivate high-order thinking skills.
Problem-solving is achieved as learner conducts research online to obtain more information about the author and the setting of the story.
sub_strands.values: Unity is enhanced as the learner develops skills for working in harmony with others while participating.
sub_strands.pcis: Creative thinking is developed as the learner creates charts to summarise what they have learned.
sub_strands.links: The learner relates the skill of intensive reading to their reading of class readers in Kiswahili.

outcomes.text: explain the different parts that aid in previewing a book
describe the author and the setting of the text in terms of time and place
underscore the value of reading for lifelong learning

skills.name: Use the parts of a book to preview it
skills.mastery: Says what the cover, title page, blurb, contents page, author's note and glossary tell the reader and which part to read first to decide on a book, and does not mix them up, in 8 of 10 new items.
question_forms: choose the part for the need
choose what the part tells you

prerequisites.reason: Grade 6 English taught it first. Proposed, to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

misconceptions.error: Thinks the blurb is the story or the contents page.

example.question: Which part of a book gives a short summary on the back cover.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "the contents page" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: The blurb is the short note on the back cover.
misconceptions.feedback: The blurb is a short note, usually on the back cover, that tells what the book is about.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Mixes up the contents page and the index.

example.question: Where do you find the list of chapters and their page numbers.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "the index" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Contents is at the front, the index is at the back.
misconceptions.feedback: The contents page, at the front, lists the chapters in order. The index, at the back, lists topics and names in alphabetical order.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Thinks the title page tells the story.

example.question: Which part tells the author's name and the publisher.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "the glossary" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: The title page shows who wrote and published the book.
misconceptions.feedback: The title page gives the title, the author and often the publisher.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Thinks the glossary is a list of the chapters.

example.question: Where would you find the meaning of a hard word used in the book.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "the contents page" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: A glossary explains hard words.
misconceptions.feedback: A glossary at the back of a book explains the hard or special words used in it.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

sub_strands.sub_strand: Mechanics of Writing: Punctuation Marks (Theme 2: Science and health education)
learning_experiences: read print or non-print texts and identify the full stop, exclamation mark, and question mark,
punctuate a text using the target punctuation marks,
write a short story or dialogue on the theme of science and health education using the full stop, exclamation mark, and question mark, where necessary,
engage in online or offline punctuation games with peers,
create and display posters or charts with punctuated sentences for peer review and revision,
role-play well-punctuated dialogues and record,
discuss the effectiveness of punctuation marks in expressing meaning.
key_inquiry_questions: Why is it important to punctuate a text?
sub_strands.core_competences:
Digital literacy: It is developed as learners use digital devices as they play online games and record dialogues.
Self-efficacy is achieved as learners pay attention to detail while role-playing and recording dialogues.
sub_strands.values: Unity is achieved as learners give each other feedback on charts and posters featuring the use of punctuation marks.
sub_strands.pcis:
Effective communication is exhibited through well-punctuated texts.
Social skills are enhanced as learners discuss the effectiveness of punctuation marks in expressing meaning.
sub_strands.links: The learner relates the concept of proper punctuation in other learning areas such as Kiswahili.

outcomes.text: recognise the full stop, exclamation mark, and question mark in texts
use the full stop, exclamation mark, and question mark in sentences
acknowledge the importance of punctuating sentences accurately

skills.name: Use the full stop, question mark and exclamation mark
skills.mastery: Ends a statement with a full stop, a question with a question mark and a strong feeling or command with an exclamation mark, and does not use a question mark after a reported question, in 8 of 10 new items.

prerequisites.reason: Grade 5 English taught it first. Proposed, to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.
Grade 6 English taught it first. Proposed, to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

misconceptions.error: Ends a statement or a reported question with a question mark (He asked where I was going?).

example.question: Which sentence is correct.
example.wrong_answer: She asked me where I was going?
example.correct_answer: She asked me where I was going.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "She asked me where I was going?" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: A question mark is for the exact question, not for a sentence that tells about it.
misconceptions.feedback: A sentence that reports a question tells what was asked, so it ends with a full stop.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Ends a real question with a full stop (Where is the market.).

example.question: Which sentence is correct.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Where is the market." next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: A sentence that asks something ends with a question mark.
misconceptions.feedback: A direct question ends with a question mark, not a full stop.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Uses a full stop where a strong feeling or a command needs an exclamation mark (Watch out.)

example.question: Which sentence is correct.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Watch out." next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: A shout or sudden warning takes an exclamation mark.
misconceptions.feedback: An exclamation mark shows a strong feeling or a sudden command or warning: Watch out! What a surprise!
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Writes several marks together (Help!!! What???).

example.question: Which sentence is correct.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Stop thief!!!" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: One mark is enough.
misconceptions.feedback: Use only one end mark. Writing three marks is not correct in school writing.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Forgets the capital letter at the start of the next sentence after an end mark.

example.question: Which is correct.
example.wrong_answer: It was late. we went home.
example.correct_answer: It was late. We went home.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "It was late. we went home." next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: A new sentence begins with a capital letter.
misconceptions.feedback: After a full stop, question mark or exclamation mark a new sentence starts with a capital letter.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

sub_strands.sub_strand: Listening for the main idea (Theme 3: Hygiene)
learning_experiences: listen to audio recordings on hygiene and identify the main idea,
listen for specific information from the audio recording on hygiene and take notes,
search online and offline for expressions that signal the main ideas, such as; this talk is about... I will talk about...,
watch a video describing a process, a person, or an object and pick out specific information,
listen to peers read descriptive texts, and note down the main ideas in turns.
key_inquiry_questions: What can you do to ensure you capture the main ideas from a speaker?
sub_strands.core_competences:
Communication : It is enhanced as the learner listens keenly and responds to descriptive texts.
Digital literacy is achieved as the learner uses digital devices to search online for expressions that signal the main idea and specific information.
sub_strands.values: Respect is enhanced as the learner listens keenly to peers reading descriptive texts and noting the main ideas.
sub_strands.pcis: Health education - personal hygiene is promoted as the learner listens to audio texts on hygiene.
sub_strands.links: Learners relate to concepts in Agriculture as they listen to a recording on hygiene.

outcomes.text: identify the main idea from varied descriptive texts
pick out specific information from varied descriptive texts
acknowledge the importance of listening skills in communication

sub_strands.sub_strand: Reading: Information and Meaning (Theme 3: Hygiene)
learning_experiences: distinguish between reading for information and reading for meaning,
collaborate with peers to scan through a text and identify text features (such as title, subtitles),
read texts on issues such as hygiene, safety, and security and organise the information by making notes,
infer and share, the meaning of words from varied texts,
use the words to construct sentences to convey information and meaning,
fill in crossword puzzles using words learned.
key_inquiry_questions: How would you tell the meaning of a word in a passage?
sub_strands.core_competences: Collaboration: It is promoted as the learner infers and shares the meaning of words.
sub_strands.values: Respect is enhanced as the learner shares ideas as they work with peers to infer meanings of words
sub_strands.pcis: Health and Safety is achieved as the learner reads texts on issues such as hygiene, safety, and security
sub_strands.links: The learner relates the skill of reading for information and meaning to other language learning areas such as Kiswahili.

outcomes.text: distinguish between reading for information and reading for meaning
infer the meaning of words and phrases from varied texts
appreciate the importance of reading for information and meaning

skills.name: Tell reading for information from reading for meaning
skills.mastery: Says that reading for information is to find facts (a timetable, a notice) and reading for meaning is to understand and enjoy what the writer says (a story, a poem), and chooses which to do for a task, in 8 of 10 new items.
question_forms: choose the way to read for the task

prerequisites.reason: Grade 6 English taught it first. Proposed, to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

misconceptions.error: Thinks reading a timetable is reading for meaning.

example.question: You read a bus timetable to find when the next bus leaves. Which kind of reading is this.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "reading for meaning" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: You are looking for a fact.
misconceptions.feedback: Reading for information is to find facts. Reading for meaning is to understand and enjoy what the writer means.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Thinks a story is read only for information.

example.question: Which text is mainly read for meaning and enjoyment.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "a notice board" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: A story is read to enjoy and understand.
misconceptions.feedback: Stories and poems are read mainly for meaning and enjoyment. Notices, timetables and maps are read for information.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Reads the whole text slowly when only one fact is needed.

example.question: You need the date on a poster. What is the quickest way.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "read every word slowly" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Look for the one fact you need.
misconceptions.feedback: When you read for information, scan quickly for the fact you need. Reading for meaning is slower and fuller.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

sub_strands.sub_strand: Verbs and Tense (Theme 3: Hygiene)
learning_experiences: search online and offline for information on verbs and their tenses,
listen to texts read by the teacher on verbs and their tenses,
identify and group verbs with similar endings such as: -ing, -ed, -ied, -d from passages on the theme of hygiene,
identify the tenses of the verbs in sentences,
construct sentences using verbs in the correct tenses,
participate in a language game on tenses,
engage in conversations in pairs using verbs in various tenses,
review their peers’ use of tense in the conversations and give feedback.
key_inquiry_questions: Why is it important to use correct tenses in communication?
sub_strands.core_competences: Communication and collaboration: It is developed as the learner engages in conversations in pairs using verbs in various tenses.
sub_strands.values: Respect is inculcated as the learner reviews peers’ use of tenses.
sub_strands.pcis: Effective communication is enhanced as the learner constructs sentences using verbs and tenses correctly.
sub_strands.links: The learner relates the correct use of verbs and tenses to correct language use when writing their essays in subjects such as Religious Education.

outcomes.text: identify regular and irregular verbs in sentences
use regular and irregular verbs to construct sentences using the past, present, and future tenses
appreciate the correct use of verbs and tenses for effective communication

skills.name: Use regular and irregular verbs in the past and the past participle
skills.mastery: Writes the past form (went, saw, ate) and the past participle (gone, seen, eaten) of common irregular verbs, tells them from regular verbs that add -ed, and does not write goed, seen for saw or have went, in 8 of 10 new items.

skills.name: Choose the present, past or future tense from the time in the sentence
skills.mastery: Uses the time word (every day, yesterday, next week) to choose the present, past or future form, and does not write yesterday I go or tomorrow I went, in 8 of 10 new items.

prerequisites.reason: This skill builds on it. Proposed, to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.
Grade 5 English taught it first. Proposed, to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

misconceptions.error: Adds -ed to an irregular verb (goed, eated, buyed, thinked).

example.question: Yesterday we ___ to the lake.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "goed" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Go is an irregular verb. Its past is went.
misconceptions.feedback: Irregular verbs do not take -ed. The past of go is went, of eat is ate, of buy is bought and of think is thought.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Uses the past form where the past participle is needed (has went, have saw, had ate).

example.question: The bell has already ___.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "rang" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: After has, have or had, use the past participle: has rung.
misconceptions.feedback: After has, have and had use the past participle: has gone, have seen, had eaten. The past form (went, saw, ate) is used alone.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Uses the participle for the plain past (I seen it, she done it, we gone home).

example.question: I ___ the lion yesterday.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "seen" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Without has, have or had, use the past form: I saw.
misconceptions.feedback: Used alone, the verb takes its past form: I saw, she did, we went. The participle (seen, done, gone) needs has, have or had in front of it.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Makes a regular verb irregular or an irregular verb regular (runned, swimmed, but wented).

example.question: Our teacher ___ us a story last week.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "telled" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Tell is irregular: told.
misconceptions.feedback: The past of tell is told, of teach is taught, of bring is brought. Regular verbs such as walk and cook take -ed.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Uses the present with a past time word (Yesterday I go to the market).

example.question: Yesterday, Atieno ___ to the market.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "goes" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Yesterday is past time, so the verb is in the past.
misconceptions.feedback: A time word such as yesterday or last week shows the past, so the verb must be in the past tense.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Uses the past with a future time word (Tomorrow we went to Mombasa).

example.question: Tomorrow we ___ to Mombasa.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "went" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Tomorrow has not happened, so the verb is in the future.
misconceptions.feedback: A time word such as tomorrow or next week shows the future, so use will + the plain verb.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Uses will with a past form (will went, will came).

example.question: Next week our class ___ a trip.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "will took" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: After will, the plain verb is used: will take.
misconceptions.feedback: After will, use the plain verb, without -s, -ed or the past form: will take, will go, will come.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Uses the continuous for a habit (She is going to church every Sunday).

example.question: Every Sunday, Mama ___ to church.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "is going" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: A habit that happens again and again uses the simple present.
misconceptions.feedback: For something that happens again and again, with words such as every day or always, use the simple present: She goes.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Chooses a tense that does not fit the time word (a continuous or participle form where a simple tense is needed).

example.question: Last Saturday we ___ the maize.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "harvesting" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Match the verb to the time word.
misconceptions.feedback: The time word shows the tense: last Saturday needs the simple past, every day the simple present, next week will + the plain verb.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

sub_strands.sub_strand: Intensive Reading: Poetry (Theme 3: Hygiene)
learning_experiences: source online or offline for different poems and note the titles and the poets while observing integrity and cyber safety,
brainstorm on the parts of a poem,
read short poems addressing issues such as personal hygiene, HIV and AIDS, and COVID-19,
analyse how poems are broken into stanzas and stanzas into lines,
study varied poems and present their different structures using graphic organisers,
compare the structures of different poems,
relate the poem’s structure to the poem’s message.
key_inquiry_questions: Why do people write poems?
What makes a poem interesting?
sub_strands.core_competences: Digital literacy: It is achieved as the learner uses digital devices to search sources online for different poems and notes the titles and the poets, while observing cyber safety.
sub_strands.values: Integrity is achieved as the learner searches online or offline for poems while observing cyber security.
sub_strands.pcis:
Health Education is promoted as the learner tackles poems on issues such as personal hygiene, HIVand AIDS, and COVID-19
Cyber Safety is promoted as the learner searches online or offline for poems.
sub_strands.links: The learner relates the structure of poems to other learning areas such as Kiswahili and Creative Arts and Sports.

outcomes.text: explain the structure of poems
analyse the structure of varied simple poems
read short poems addressing varied societal issues
appreciate the poem’s structure in communicating a message

skills.name: Describe the structure of a poem: line, stanza, rhyme and refrain
skills.mastery: Counts the lines and the stanzas of a poem, finds the words that rhyme by sound (not spelling), the line or words that repeat (the refrain), and tells a poem from a story by its shape, in 8 of 10 new items.

prerequisites.reason: Grade 6 English taught it first. Proposed, to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

leads_to.reason: Grade 8 English builds on this skill. Proposed, to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

misconceptions.error: Calls a line a stanza or a stanza a line.

example.question: What is a group of lines in a poem called.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "a line" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: A stanza is a group of lines.
misconceptions.feedback: A line is one row of words in a poem. A stanza is a group of lines, like a paragraph in prose.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Chooses rhyming words by spelling instead of sound (cough and through).

example.question: Which pair rhymes.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "cough and through" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Say the words aloud.
misconceptions.feedback: Rhyming words have the same sound at the end, even if the spelling differs. Cough and through do not rhyme.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Does not see the refrain (the repeated line or words).

example.question: What is a refrain.
example.correct_answer: a line that comes back again and again

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "the last line" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: A refrain is repeated.
misconceptions.feedback: A refrain is a line or group of words repeated in a poem or song, usually after each stanza.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Calls a poem a story because it tells something, or a story a poem.

example.question: Which is a poem.
example.wrong_answer: Our class went to the farm. We saw cows.
example.correct_answer: Sun on the hills, sun on the river, / light in the morning, light for ever.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Our class went to the farm. We saw cows." next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: A poem is set in lines with rhythm and often rhyme.
misconceptions.feedback: A poem is written in short lines and stanzas, with rhythm and often rhyme. Prose is written in sentences and paragraphs.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Counts the number of stanzas or lines wrongly.

example.question: How many stanzas does the poem have.
example.correct_answer: the number of groups of lines

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "the number of lines" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Count the groups separated by a gap.
misconceptions.feedback: Count the stanzas by the gaps between them, not by the number of lines.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

sub_strands.sub_strand: Writing Narrative Paragraphs (Theme 3: Hygiene)
learning_experiences: identify parts of a well-written paragraph specifically, an introduction, necessary details, and a conclusion,
read samples of narrative paragraphs provided by the teacher and discuss the flow of ideas,
write a paragraph using a digital device about issues such as hygiene, safety, and security,
present the paragraphs in class for peer review.
key_inquiry_questions: Why do we write paragraphs?
sub_strands.core_competences:
Communication: It is enhanced as the learner composes a narrative paragraph and reviews peers’ work.
Creativity and imagination: It is developed as the learner writes narrative paragraphs and shares with peers.
sub_strands.values: Respect is promoted as the learner gives feedback on the narrative paragraphs they have reviewed.
sub_strands.pcis: Social cohesion is enhanced as the learner presents the narrative paragraph for peer review.
sub_strands.links: The learner relates the use of digital devices to other learning areas such as Pre-Technical.

outcomes.text: identify the parts of a narrative paragraph
compose a narrative paragraph with the appropriate structure
acknowledge the significance of paragraphing in written communication

skills.name: Know the parts of a narrative paragraph
skills.mastery: Names the parts of a narrative paragraph (the opening that sets the scene, the events in order, the closing) and tells which sentence plays which part, and which does not belong, in 8 of 10 new items.

prerequisites.reason: Grade 6 English taught it first. Proposed, to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

misconceptions.error: Chooses an event from the middle for the opening of a narrative paragraph.

example.question: Which sentence best opens a narrative paragraph about a school trip.
example.correct_answer: On Friday morning our class set off for Nakuru.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Suddenly the bus broke down." next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: The opening sets the scene: who, where, when.
misconceptions.feedback: A narrative paragraph opens by setting the scene (who, where and when). The events follow in order.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Puts the events out of order.

example.question: Which sentence comes last in the paragraph.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "First we ate lunch." next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Look for the closing: finally, at last, in the end.
misconceptions.feedback: Events are told in the order they happened. Words such as first, then, after that and finally show the order.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Keeps a sentence that is about something else in the paragraph.

example.question: Which sentence does not belong in the paragraph.
example.wrong_answer: My uncle sells shoes in Eldoret.
example.correct_answer: We paid the fare and sat down.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "My uncle sells shoes in Eldoret." next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Every sentence must belong to the same story.
misconceptions.feedback: Every sentence in a narrative paragraph is part of the same story. A sentence about something else does not belong.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Ends the paragraph in the middle of the action with no closing.

example.question: Which sentence best closes the paragraph.
example.correct_answer: We were tired but happy when we got home.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Then the driver turned left." next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: A closing tells how the events ended or how the people felt.
misconceptions.feedback: A narrative paragraph ends with a closing sentence that tells how it all ended or what the person felt.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

sub_strands.sub_strand: Listening Comprehension: Selective Listening (Theme 4: Leadership)
learning_experiences: listen to an audio text and decide whether the information presented is specific or general,
search online for audio recordings on leadership and attentively listen to texts for specific information,
watch a role play and respond to questions,
listen to a passage on leadership (good governance) and answer questions posed by the speaker.
key_inquiry_questions: What can you do to ensure you capture relevant information from a speaker?
sub_strands.core_competences: Critical Thinking is developed as the learner listens and selects general and specific information from oral texts.
sub_strands.values:
Integrity: It is promoted as the learner nurtures discipline while listening to texts on good governance.
Social justice: It is enhanced as the learner learns the need for fairness while listening to oral texts on leadership.
sub_strands.pcis:
Good governance is enhanced as the learner listens to texts on leadership.
Effective communication is achieved as the learner listens and responds to audio texts on good governance.
sub_strands.links: The learner relates selective listening to their learning in Kiswahili.

outcomes.text: distinguish between specific and general information from a listening text
select specific information from a listening text
listen and respond to texts on leadership
emphasise the value of listening skills in communication

skills.name: Tell specific from general information and pick out the details
skills.mastery: Says whether a question asks for the general idea or for a specific detail (a name, a number, a place, a time), and picks out the specific detail from a short text read to or by the learner, in 8 of 10 new items.

prerequisites.reason: Grade 6 English taught it first. Proposed, to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

leads_to.reason: Grade 8 English builds on this skill. Proposed, to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

misconceptions.error: Takes a detail for the general idea.

example.question: Which is a question about the general idea of a text on Lake Victoria.
example.wrong_answer: How deep is the lake at its deepest point?
example.correct_answer: What is the text mostly about?

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "How deep is the lake at its deepest point?" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: A general question asks about the whole text.
misconceptions.feedback: A general question asks what the whole text is about. A specific question asks for one detail such as a name, number, place or time.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Takes the general idea for a specific detail.

example.question: Which question asks for a specific detail.
example.correct_answer: On what date did the festival begin?

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "What is the text about?" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: A specific question has a short, exact answer.
misconceptions.feedback: A specific question asks for a name, a number, a place or a time that is in the text.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Picks a detail that is near the answer but is not what was asked.

example.question: The text says the match started at two and ended at four. At what time did the match end.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "two o'clock" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Match the question word: ended asks for the end.
misconceptions.feedback: Read the question word carefully. The match started at two, but the question asks when it ended: four o'clock.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Gives a number from the wrong place in the text.

example.question: The text says 40 learners went on the trip and 5 teachers. How many teachers went.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "40" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Find the number that goes with the noun asked.
misconceptions.feedback: Several numbers may be in the text. Choose the number that goes with the noun in the question.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

sub_strands.sub_strand: Intensive Reading (Theme 4: Leadership)
learning_experiences: search online and watch appropriate video clips on the selected reading strategies: reading for main ideas and reading for details,
read and underline the main ideas and details in texts on issues such as gender roles in leadership, and review each other’s work,
share ideas on how they can use the selected reading strategies,
fill in substitution tables with specific details from texts, in pairs,
complete a mind map with a focus on the main idea and details.
key_inquiry_questions: How can you improve your reading?
sub_strands.core_competences:
Learning to learn: It is developed as the learner shares what they have learnt using a mind map showing the main idea and details.
Digital literacy is enhanced as the learner manipulates digital devices while searching online and watching appropriate video clips on the selected reading strategies.
sub_strands.values: Unity is achieved as the learner works together with peers to complete the mind map.
sub_strands.pcis: Gender roles in leadership are enhanced as the learner reads and underlines the main ideas and details in texts focusing on leadership.
sub_strands.links: The learner relates the skill of selecting main idea and specific details to learning areas such as Religious Education.

outcomes.text: discuss the identified reading strategies
select main ideas and details from a variety of written texts
acknowledge the importance of reading for main idea and details as a comprehension skill

skills.name: Choose a reading strategy for a purpose: skimming, scanning, predicting, rereading
skills.mastery: Chooses skimming for a quick idea of a text, scanning for a name or number, predicting from the title and clues, and rereading with the words around a hard sentence, and names the strategy from what the reader does, in 8 of 10 new items.
question_forms: choose the strategy for the purpose
