prerequisites.reason: Grade 5 English taught it first. Proposed, to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

leads_to.reason: Grade 8 English builds on this skill. Proposed, to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

misconceptions.error: Mixes up skimming and scanning.

example.question: You want to find one name quickly in a long text. Which strategy is best.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "skimming" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Scanning looks for one fact. Skimming gets the general idea.
misconceptions.feedback: Skimming is reading quickly to get the general idea. Scanning is running the eye over a text to find one name, number or fact.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Chooses something that is not a strategy (guessing, skipping, reading aloud every word) for the purpose.

example.question: You do not understand a sentence. Which strategy helps.
example.correct_answer: reading it again with the words around it

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "skipping it" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: A reading strategy helps you to understand.
misconceptions.feedback: Rereading the sentence and the words around it, predicting, skimming and scanning are strategies. Skipping and guessing are not.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

sub_strands.sub_strand: Verbs and Tense (Theme 4: Leadership)
learning_experiences: underline verbs in simple present and simple past tense in a text,
reflect on the formation of simple present and simple past tense forms of verbs,
construct and share sentences on a variety of issues, including leadership, using verbs in the appropriate tense,
type the constructed sentences using a digital device,
search online or offline for verbs used in simple present and simple past tense from a variety of texts,
complete sentences using the correct tense of the given verbs,
create and display charts showing words in their simple present and past tense,
play language games using verbs in the present and past tense.
key_inquiry_questions: Why is it necessary to indicate when an activity takes place?
sub_strands.core_competences: Self-efficacy: It is developed as the learner builds on their learning experiences while constructing grammatically correct sentences and using them in oral communication.
sub_strands.values: Integrity is enhanced as the learner constructs sentences on leadership.
sub_strands.pcis: Effective communication is enhanced as the learner uses the appropriate tense to discuss leadership. Good governance is enhanced as the learner constructs sentences on leadership.
sub_strands.links: The learner relates the concept of tense to their learning in Kiswahili.

outcomes.text: identify verbs in the simple present and simple past tense in a text
write sentences using the simple present tense
write sentences using the simple past tense
advocate appropriate use of tense in communication

skills.name: Write the simple present tense
skills.mastery: Writes the simple present for habits and facts, adds -s or -es after he, she, it or one name (She walks, he washes), uses do not and does not with the plain verb, and does not write he walk or she do not know, in 8 of 10 new items.

skills.name: Write the simple past tense
skills.mastery: Writes the simple past with -ed (with the spelling changes stopped, studied) or the irregular form, uses did not and did with the plain verb, and does not write did not went or she walkd, in 8 of 10 new items.

prerequisites.reason: This skill builds on it. Proposed, to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

misconceptions.error: Leaves out -s after he, she, it or a single name (She walk to school).

example.question: Wanjiru ___ to school every day.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "walk" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: One person (she, he, it) takes -s or -es on the verb in the simple present.
misconceptions.feedback: In the simple present, a verb after he, she, it or one name ends in -s or -es: she walks, he washes.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Adds -s after I, you, we or they (They plays, we likes).

example.question: The boys ___ football after lessons.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "plays" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: With a plural subject the verb has no -s.
misconceptions.feedback: With I, you, we, they and plural nouns the verb stays plain: the boys play.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Adds -s to the verb after does (She does not walks).

example.question: My brother does not ___ coffee.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "drinks" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: After do or does the plain verb is used: does not drink.
misconceptions.feedback: After do not and does not the verb is plain, because does already carries the -s: He does not drink.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Uses do not after he, she or it (She do not know).

example.question: Our neighbour ___ not own a car.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "do" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: One person takes does, not do.
misconceptions.feedback: After he, she, it or one name, use does not (not do not): She does not know.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Adds only -s after ch, sh, s, x, o, or y after a consonant (she washs, he trys).

example.question: The cook ___ the dishes after supper.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "washs" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: After sh, ch, s, x and o, add -es. After a consonant and y, y becomes ies.
misconceptions.feedback: Verbs that end in sh, ch, s, x or o add -es (washes, teaches, goes). A consonant and y change to ies (try, tries).
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Puts the past form after did (Did you went? She did not came).

example.question: Did you ___ the match yesterday?

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "watched" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Did already shows the past, so the verb is plain.
misconceptions.feedback: After did and did not, use the plain verb: Did you watch? She did not come. Did already shows the past.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Leaves the verb plain in a past story (Yesterday she walk home).

example.question: Last Saturday we ___ the maize.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "harvest" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Last Saturday is past. A regular verb adds -ed.
misconceptions.feedback: A regular verb in the past ends in -ed: harvested, walked, cooked.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Spells -ed wrongly (stoped, studyed, plaied).

example.question: The driver ___ at the junction.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "stoped" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: A short verb with one vowel and one consonant doubles the last letter before -ed.
misconceptions.feedback: Spelling changes before -ed: stop, stopped (double the p); study, studied (y becomes i); play, played (no change after a vowel).
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Uses was with you, we or they, or were with I, he, she, it (We was late).

example.question: The children ___ happy to see the visitors.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "was" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: A plural subject takes were.
misconceptions.feedback: Was goes with I, he, she, it and one name. Were goes with you, we, they and plural nouns.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Uses an -ing or a past form where the simple present is needed.

example.question: My sister ___ to music while she studies.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "listening" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: A habit uses the simple present.
misconceptions.feedback: For a habit or a fact use the simple present: she listens, they play. An -ing form needs is, are or am in front of it.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

sub_strands.sub_strand: Intensive Reading: Class Readers (Theme 4: Leadership)
learning_experiences: read a section of a class reader and identify the main characters,
discuss predictions made from the title and the sections read,
participate in a reader’s theatre and read portions of the class reader,
outline the things done by each character studied in the section,
discuss how the characters make the story flow,
write a summary about how the main characters make the story flow.
key_inquiry_questions: What would you consider when selecting a storybook to read?
sub_strands.core_competences:
Learning to learn:It is developed as the learner shares ideas on how the characters make the story flow.
Critical thinking:It is developed as the learner makes predictions from the title and the section read.
sub_strands.values: Responsibility is enhanced as the learner writes a summary based on the main character.
sub_strands.pcis: Critical thinking is enhanced as the learner discusses how characters contribute to the flow of the story.
sub_strands.links: The learner relates the concept of prediction to their learning in Integrated Science.

outcomes.text: identify the main characters in a text
explain how the characters make the story flow
make predictions based on the title and the sections read
appreciate the role of characters in the class reader

skills.name: Name the main and minor characters and what each does in a story
skills.mastery: Names the main character (the story is about the person) and a minor character (helps or gets in the way) from a short story, and says what the character does to move the story on, in 8 of 10 new items.

prerequisites.reason: Grade 6 English taught it first. Proposed, to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

skills.name: Judge a character from what the person says and does
skills.mastery: Chooses the trait that a character's words and actions support (brave, selfish, honest, jealous), and the line that is the evidence, and does not judge from the name or one word, in 8 of 10 new items.

prerequisites.reason: Grade 6 English taught it first. Proposed, to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

leads_to.reason: Grade 8 English builds on this skill. Proposed, to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

skills.name: Predict what happens next from the title and the clues
skills.mastery: Uses the title and the clues so far to choose the most likely next event and says which clue supports it, in 8 of 10 new passages.
question_forms: choose the clue that supports it

prerequisites.reason: Grade 6 English taught it first. Proposed, to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.
This skill builds on it. Proposed, to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

misconceptions.error: Names a minor character as the main character.

example.question: Who is the main character of the story.
example.wrong_answer: a character who only appears once
example.correct_answer: the person the story is about

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "a character who only appears once" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: The main character is in most of the story.
misconceptions.feedback: The main character is the person the story is mostly about. A minor character helps the story but is not the centre of it.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Names the main character when a minor one is asked.

example.question: Who is a minor character in the story.
example.wrong_answer: the girl the story is about
example.correct_answer: the shopkeeper who sells her the bread

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "the girl the story is about" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: A minor character plays a small part.
misconceptions.feedback: A minor character has a small part and is not the centre of the story.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Names a place, an object or an event as a character.

example.question: Who is a character in the story.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "the village" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: A character is a person or an animal that acts.
misconceptions.feedback: A character is a person or an animal in the story. A place is the setting.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Says the wrong thing about what a character does in the story.

example.question: What does the character do to move the story on.
example.correct_answer: the thing the character does in the passage

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "something done by another character" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Find the line where the character acts.
misconceptions.feedback: A character moves the story on by what the character says or does. Check who does the action.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Chooses the opposite trait to the one the actions show.

example.question: Which word best describes the character.
example.wrong_answer: the opposite of the right word

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "the opposite of the right word" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Look at what the person does.
misconceptions.feedback: A trait is shown by what a character says and does. Choose the word that fits the actions.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Judges a character by the name or one word.

example.question: Which word describes the character.
example.wrong_answer: a trait chosen from the name

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "a trait chosen from the name" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Do not judge from the name.
misconceptions.feedback: Judge a character by what the person does and says, not by the name or one word.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Chooses a line that does not show the trait as evidence.

example.question: Which line shows the trait.
example.correct_answer: a line about what the character does

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "a line about the setting" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Evidence is something the character says or does.
misconceptions.feedback: The evidence for a trait is a line that shows what the character says or does. A line about the setting or the time is not evidence.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Predicts something with no clue in the passage.

example.question: What will probably happen next.
example.correct_answer: an event the clues point to

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "an event with no clue" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: A prediction needs a clue.
misconceptions.feedback: A good prediction is supported by a clue in the passage.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Predicts something that goes against the passage.

example.question: What will probably happen next.
example.correct_answer: an event that fits the story

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "an event against the story" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: The prediction must agree with what has been told.
misconceptions.feedback: A prediction must fit what the passage has already told us.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Chooses an event that has already happened.

example.question: What will probably happen next.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "an event already told" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: A prediction is about what has not happened yet.
misconceptions.feedback: A prediction is about what comes next, not about what has already happened.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Chooses a sentence that is not a clue for the prediction.

example.question: Which sentence is the best clue for the prediction.
example.correct_answer: a sentence that points to the prediction

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "a sentence about something else" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Ask: which sentence makes this likely.
misconceptions.feedback: A clue is a sentence that points to what will happen next.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

sub_strands.sub_strand: Paragraphing: Using examples and incidents (Theme 4: Leadership)
learning_experiences: share ideas on examples and incidents that can be included in a paragraph,
collaborate with peers to develop a paragraph on leadership using the ideas generated in their earlier discussion,
present their paragraphs in class for peer review,
use mind maps to generate examples and incidents for sample paragraphs,
compose a paragraph based on suggested examples and incidents.
key_inquiry_questions: How can you organise your ideas logically?
sub_strands.core_competences: Creativity and imagination: It is enhanced as the learner creates a paragraph and makes connections between similar and related incidents.
sub_strands.values: Love is enhanced as the learner shows care and compassion when reviewing paragraphs written by peers.
sub_strands.pcis: Diversity is developed as the learner collaborates with others to create a paragraph on leadership.
sub_strands.links: Kiswahili and Social Studies require learner to organise ideas in paragraphs.

outcomes.text: outline examples and incidents to include in a paragraph
create a well-developed paragraph using examples and incidents
appreciate the importance of well-written paragraphs in writing

skills.name: Support a paragraph with examples and incidents
skills.mastery: Chooses the example or incident that supports the topic sentence, tells it from a sentence that is off the topic, and says which words introduce an example (for example, for instance), in 8 of 10 new items.
question_forms: find the sentence that does not belong

prerequisites.reason: This skill builds on it. Proposed, to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.
Grade 6 English taught it first. Proposed, to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

misconceptions.error: Chooses an example that is about something else.

example.question: Topic: Our school keeps the compound clean. Which sentence gives a good example.
example.wrong_answer: Our school has a big football field.
example.correct_answer: Every Friday each class sweeps its own corner.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Our school has a big football field." next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: An example must show the topic sentence is true.
misconceptions.feedback: An example must show that the topic sentence is true. A fact about something else does not support it.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Repeats the topic sentence in other words instead of giving an example.

example.question: Which sentence is an example.
example.correct_answer: Last term our school won the cleanest compound prize.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Our school is very clean." next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: An example gives a real case, not the same idea again.
misconceptions.feedback: An example names a real case or incident. Saying the same thing again in other words is not an example.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Chooses the wrong words to bring in an example (However, as a result, finally).

example.question: Which words bring in an example.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "However" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: For example and for instance bring in an example.
misconceptions.feedback: For example, for instance and such as bring in an example. However shows a contrast.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Thinks a general statement is an incident.

example.question: Which sentence tells an incident.
example.correct_answer: Yesterday a boy found a purse and took it to the teacher.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Children like to play." next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: An incident is one thing that happened at one time.
misconceptions.feedback: An incident is one event that happened at a time and place. A general statement is not an incident.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Keeps a sentence about something else in the paragraph, or takes a sentence that belongs for the odd one.

example.question: Which sentence does not belong in the paragraph.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "a sentence that belongs" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Every sentence must be about the topic.
misconceptions.feedback: Every sentence of a paragraph must be about the same topic. The sentence about something else does not belong.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

sub_strands.sub_strand: Pronunciation: Sounds and Word Stress (Theme 5: Family)
learning_experiences: pronounce the consonant sounds / p/, /b/, /k/ and /g/ from a text,
practise saying the short /i/ and the long /i:/ sounds in pairs,
watch and listen to an audio-visual recording featuring selected consonants and vowel sounds,
work with peers to make a recording featuring learned sounds,
practise saying words with the sounds/p/ as in pin; /b/ as in bean, /k/ as in kin; /g/ as in goat, / i/ as in bin; and /i:/ as in seen correctly,
distinguish the meaning of words based on stress, for example, project (verb) project (noun),
play language games to distinguish word meaning on basis of stress,
practise pronouncing minimal pairs containing the target sounds.
key_inquiry_questions: Why is it important to articulate sounds correctly?
sub_strands.core_competences:
Digital Literacy: It is developed as the learner selects digital technology to watch and listen to audio visual recordings on consonants and vowel sounds
Communication: It is developed as learner speaks clearly and effectively while articulating the consonant and vowel sounds correctly.
Collaboration: It is developed as the learner actively participates when making recording of the target vowel and consonant sounds.
sub_strands.values: Unity is enhanced as the learner displays a team spirit while working with peers to record words with vowel and consonant sounds.
sub_strands.pcis:
Self-esteem is enhanced as the learner practises pronunciation of vowel and consonant sounds.
Social cohesion is enhanced as the learner makes sentences on family relationships.
sub_strands.links: The learner relates the concept of correct articulation to their learning in Kiswahili.

outcomes.text: identify the consonant and vowel sounds in words
articulate consonants and vowel sounds for oral fluency
distinguish the meaning of words on the basis of stress
advocate the role of correct pronunciation in communication

sub_strands.sub_strand: Synonyms and Antonyms (Theme 5: Family)
learning_experiences: use reference materials such as the encyclopaedia and the dictionary to locate synonyms and antonyms,
check the meaning and pronunciation of synonyms and antonyms from the dictionary,
search for synonyms and antonyms from print and digital texts,
create a crossword puzzle using synonyms and antonyms and share it online,
use synonyms and antonyms in sentences,
match words with their antonyms from a list of words,
practise pronouncing synonyms and antonyms in pairs,
design and display a chart with antonyms and synonyms of words correctly spelled.
key_inquiry_questions: Why do we use antonyms and synonyms?
sub_strands.core_competences:
Digital Literacy:It is developed as the learner interacts with digital devices and uses them to access an online encyclopedia and dictionary.
Learning to learn is enhanced as learners work independently when looking up the meanings of words in the dictionary and encyclopedia.
sub_strands.values: Patriotism is enhanced as the learner gains a sense of belonging to the family while constructing sentences using synonyms and antonyms about family.
sub_strands.pcis: Social cohesion is enhanced as learners construct sentences on varied issues such as family set- up using synonyms and antonyms of words.
sub_strands.links: The learner relates the concept of synonyms and antonyms to their learning of vocabulary in Kiswahili.

outcomes.text: identify synonyms and antonyms of words from written texts
spell synonyms and antonyms correctly for writing fluency
use synonyms and antonyms in sentences
appreciate the importance of correct use of words in communication

sub_strands.sub_strand: Comparative and Superlative Adjectives (Theme 5: Family)
learning_experiences: identify comparative and superlative adjectives from texts, in pairs,
search online or offline for examples of comparative and superlative adjectives,
construct sentences using comparative and superlative adjectives,
play language games featuring adjectives,
use a substitution table to complete sentences featuring comparative and superlative adjectives,
use flashcards to categorise comparative and superlative adjectives,
work with peers to compare various items within the environment using comparative and superlative adjectives.
key_inquiry_questions: Why is it important to make comparisons in life?
sub_strands.core_competences:
Learning to learn: It is developed as the learner organises their learning and searches online or offline for examples of comparative and superlative adjectives.
Self-efficacy: It is enhanced as the learner uses flashcards to categorise adjectives into comparatives and superlatives successfully.
sub_strands.values: Love is nurtured as the learner uses adjectives in the comparative and superlative forms to express family relations.
sub_strands.pcis: Self-awareness is enhanced as the learner identifies comparative and superlative adjectives from texts on family relationships.
sub_strands.links: The learner relates correct use of comparative and superlative forms to the editing of their written work in all learning areas including Pre-Technical Studies.

outcomes.text: identify comparative and superlative adjectives in texts
use comparative and superlative adjectives in communication
acknowledge the value of comparative and superlative forms of adjectives in communication

skills.name: Use comparative and superlative adjectives
skills.mastery: Writes -er and -est for short adjectives, more and most for long ones, the irregular forms (good, better, best; bad, worse, worst), than with the comparative and the with the superlative, and does not write more taller or the most best, in 8 of 10 new items.

prerequisites.reason: Grade 6 English taught it first. Proposed, to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.
Grade 5 English taught it first. Proposed, to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

leads_to.reason: Grade 8 English builds on this skill. Proposed, to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.
Grade 8 English builds on this skill. Proposed, to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

misconceptions.error: Uses more with -er (more taller) or most with -est (most tallest).

example.question: Kamau is ___ than his brother.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "more taller" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: A short adjective takes -er, with no more.
misconceptions.feedback: A short adjective takes -er or -est on its own: taller, tallest. Do not add more or most as well.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Adds -er or -est to a long adjective (beautifuler, expensivest).

example.question: This dress is ___ than that one.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "beautifuler" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: A long adjective takes more and most.
misconceptions.feedback: Long adjectives (beautiful, expensive, interesting) take more and most, not -er and -est.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Makes the wrong form of good, bad or far (gooder, badder, the goodest).

example.question: Her marks are ___ than mine.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "gooder" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Good is irregular: good, better, best.
misconceptions.feedback: Good, bad and far are irregular: good, better, best; bad, worse, worst; far, farther, farthest.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Uses the with the comparative or than with the superlative.

example.question: Mount Kenya is the ___ mountain in Kenya.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "higher" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: The goes with the superlative. Than goes with the comparative.
misconceptions.feedback: The superlative (highest) is used with the for one out of many. The comparative (higher) is used with than for two.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Spells the -er or -est form wrongly (bigger written biger, happier written happyer).

example.question: Today is ___ than yesterday. (hot)

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "hoter" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: A short adjective with one vowel and one consonant doubles the last letter.
misconceptions.feedback: Double the last letter of a short adjective (big, bigger; hot, hotter) and change y to i (happy, happier).
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Uses the plain adjective where the comparative or the superlative is needed (Juma is tall than Peter).

example.question: Juma is ___ than Peter.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "tall" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Than needs a comparative.
misconceptions.feedback: After than use the comparative (taller). The plain adjective (tall) is used with as ... as.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

sub_strands.sub_strand: Intensive Reading: Oral Narratives (Theme 5: Family)
learning_experiences: predict the actions of characters in legends,
read a heroic narrative- (legends) aloud in turns,
identify the characters in legends,
discuss heroic acts in the legends,
relate legends to their actions,
identify and discuss the moral lessons learned from legends,
reflect on the impact of their actions on the society,
discuss how to collect narratives from the community,
use a mind map to show how the moral lessons in the narrative can be of benefit to the community,
research and identify the community needs to be addressed through the functional reading of legend narratives,
collaborate with peers to develop legend narratives.
key_inquiry_questions: Why is it important to learn about heroes in society?
sub_strands.core_competences:
Citizenship: It is enhanced as the learner reads about legends and discusses the moral lessons learned from the legends.
Critical thinking and problem-solving: It developed as the learner prepares and studies instructions on how collecting narratives can be conducted in the community.
sub_strands.values: Patriotism is enhanced as the learner reflects on the impact of the actions of the heroes and heroines on society.
sub_strands.pcis: Creative thinking is inculcated as the learner analyses the heroic actions of the characters in the oral narratives.
sub_strands.links: The learner relates the learning of moral lessons from oral narratives to their learning in Religious Education.

outcomes.text: identify heroic characters in legends
explain the moral lessons in legends
discuss why legends are important in various communities
relate the characters in the legends to real life

skills.name: Name the hero of a legend and the lesson a story teaches
skills.mastery: Says what makes a character a hero in a legend (brave, wise, generous), and chooses the moral lesson of a story, not a detail and not a lesson the story does not teach, in 8 of 10 new items.

prerequisites.reason: Grade 6 English taught it first. Proposed, to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.
Grade 6 English taught it first. Proposed, to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

misconceptions.error: Gives a detail of the story as the lesson.

example.question: What lesson does the story teach.
example.correct_answer: a lesson about how to behave

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "a detail from the story" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: A lesson applies to real life, not only to the story.
misconceptions.feedback: The moral lesson is what the story teaches about how to behave, not a detail of what happened.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Gives a lesson that the story does not teach.

example.question: What lesson does the story teach.
example.wrong_answer: a lesson the story does not teach
example.correct_answer: the lesson the story ends with

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "a lesson the story does not teach" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Check the ending: what was the result of the choice.
misconceptions.feedback: A lesson must be shown by what happens in the story, especially the ending.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Gives the opposite of the lesson (greed pays).

example.question: What lesson does the story teach.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "the opposite of the lesson" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Ask what happened to the character who did wrong.
misconceptions.feedback: Look at what happens to the characters at the end. That shows the lesson.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Gives a quality that does not make a hero (richness, size) for the hero of a legend.

example.question: What makes the character a hero in the legend.
example.correct_answer: being brave and helping the people

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "being rich" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: A hero acts bravely for others.
misconceptions.feedback: A hero in a legend is brave, wise or generous and acts to help the people, not because of wealth or size.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

sub_strands.sub_strand: Functional Writing: Friendly Letters (Theme 5: Family)
learning_experiences: read sample friendly letters,
identify and underline parts of a friendly letter,
create a friendly letter individually,
exchange the friendly letter with a peer for feedback,
incorporate the feedback obtained from a peer,
type the friendly letter on a digital device or display the letter on a chart,
display friendly letters for other learners to give feedback.
key_inquiry_questions: Why do we write friendly letters?
sub_strands.core_competences:
Digital literacy: It is enhanced as the learner interacts with a digital device and uses it to type a friendly letter.
Communication is developed as the learner practises writing friendly letters clearly.
sub_strands.values: Respect is developed as the learner exchanges the friendly letter with a peer for feedback.
sub_strands.pcis: Creativity and imagination is enhanced as the learner writes friendly letters.
sub_strands.links: The learner relates the skill of friendly letter writing with letter writing in other languages such as Kiswahili.

outcomes.text: identify the parts of a friendly letter
compose a friendly letter using the correct format
appreciate the role of friendly letters in communication

skills.name: Know the parts of a friendly letter
skills.mastery: Puts the writer's address, date, greeting, body, closing (Your friend) and name in their places, and does not use the closing of a formal letter or write the receiver's address in a friendly letter, in 8 of 10 new items.
question_forms: choose the part and its place
find the mistake in a letter

prerequisites.reason: Grade 6 English taught it first. Proposed, to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

leads_to.reason: Grade 8 English builds on this skill. Proposed, to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

misconceptions.error: Uses a formal closing in a friendly letter (Yours faithfully to a friend).

example.question: Which closing suits a letter to your cousin.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Yours faithfully" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: A friendly letter ends warmly: Your friend, Yours lovingly.
misconceptions.feedback: A friendly letter ends in a warm way (Your friend, Your loving cousin). Yours faithfully is for formal letters.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Writes the receiver's address at the top of a friendly letter.

example.question: Which address goes at the top of a friendly letter.
example.wrong_answer: the address of the person you are writing to

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "the address of the person you are writing to" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: A friendly letter shows where the writer lives.
misconceptions.feedback: In a friendly letter the writer's address and the date go at the top right. The receiver's address goes only on the envelope.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Adds a subject line to a friendly letter.

example.question: Which part is NOT needed in a friendly letter.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "a greeting" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: A subject line belongs to a formal letter.
misconceptions.feedback: A friendly letter has the address, date, greeting, body, closing and name. A subject line is for formal letters.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Starts a friendly letter with a formal greeting (Dear Sir).

example.question: Which greeting suits a letter to your friend Achieng.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Dear Sir" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Use the name of the person you know.
misconceptions.feedback: A friendly letter begins with the name of the friend: Dear Achieng. Dear Sir is for a formal letter.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Puts the parts in the wrong order (the name before the closing).

example.question: Which part comes last in a friendly letter.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "the closing" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: The name comes after the closing.
misconceptions.feedback: The order is: address and date, greeting, body, closing, then the writer's name.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

sub_strands.sub_strand: Conversation Skills (Theme 6: Drug and substance abuse)
learning_experiences: watch a live or recorded dialogue depicting turn-taking skills and interrupting politely,
practise in pairs interrupting someone politely,
practise turn taking in a conversation with peers,
watch short videos of conversations or television programmes and identify instances of turn taking and polite interruptions,
listen to a radio talk show and pick out polite words and expressions,
write examples of polite words and expressions on sticky notes or flash cards and paste them on the wall or class noticeboard,
create posters on drug abuse and road safety showing polite expressions as well as ways of interrupting someone politely,
design posters on turn taking skills and polite interruptions and display them,
role-play a dialogue on the effects of drug and substance abuse,
recite a conversational verse (choral), make an audio or video recording and share it on WhatsApp, email, or social media.
key_inquiry_questions: How can you ensure that you do not dominate in a conversation?
How can drug and substance abuse contribute to road crashes?
sub_strands.core_competences:
Communication: It is enhanced as the learner takes turns in real life conversations and role-plays.
Collaboration is developed as the learner practises turn taking in a conversation with peers.
sub_strands.values:
Peace is enhanced as the learner practices turn taking and polite interruptions in conversations.
Respect: It is developed as the learner practises the skills of turn taking and interrupting politely.
sub_strands.pcis: Health issues are promoted as the learner role plays a dialogue on the effects of Alcohol and substance abuse.
sub_strands.links: The skills of turn taking and interrupting politely are relevant during class discussions in all subjects such as Social Studies.

outcomes.text: identify verbal and non-verbal forms of polite interruptions
apply turn-taking skills in different speaking contexts
use verbal and non-verbal cues to interrupt a conversation politely
acknowledge the importance of politeness in communication

skills.name: Interrupt politely and take turns
skills.mastery: Chooses the polite way to interrupt (Excuse me, may I say something?), to wait for a turn and to give one, tells it from a rude way, and says which gestures show politeness, in 8 of 10 new items.

prerequisites.reason: Grade 6 English taught it first. Proposed, to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

leads_to.reason: Grade 8 English builds on this skill. Proposed, to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

misconceptions.error: Interrupts with a command (Stop talking, let me speak).

example.question: Which is a polite way to interrupt a speaker.
example.correct_answer: Excuse me, may I say something?

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Stop! Let me talk now." next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Ask permission and use please or excuse me.
misconceptions.feedback: Interrupt politely with Excuse me or Sorry to interrupt and ask permission to speak.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Interrupts without waiting for a pause in the talk.

example.question: When is the best moment to join a conversation.
example.wrong_answer: while someone is in the middle of a sentence

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "while someone is in the middle of a sentence" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Wait for a pause before you ask for a turn.
misconceptions.feedback: Wait for a pause, then show you wish to speak with a small gesture or an Excuse me.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Thinks a non-verbal cue is something said.

example.question: Which is a non-verbal way to ask for a turn.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "saying Excuse me" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Non-verbal means without words.
misconceptions.feedback: A non-verbal cue is made without words: a raised hand, a nod or leaning forward. Verbal cues are spoken.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Does not give the other person a turn after speaking.

example.question: After you have given your point in a group talk, what do you do.
example.correct_answer: invite the next person to speak

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "keep talking" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Turn taking means everyone speaks in turn.
misconceptions.feedback: Turn taking means each person speaks in turn. After your point, you give the next person a chance.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

skills.name: Use adverbs of time, place and manner in sentences

This skill builds on it. Proposed, to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

misconceptions.error: Calls an adverb of time an adverb of manner, or the other way round.

example.question: In "She arrived yesterday", what does yesterday tell us.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "how" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Ask: when, where or how? Yesterday answers when.
misconceptions.feedback: An adverb of time tells when (yesterday, soon, later). An adverb of manner tells how (slowly, carefully).
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Calls an adverb of place an adverb of time (here, outside).

example.question: In "The children played outside", what does outside tell us.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "when" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Outside tells where the children played.
misconceptions.feedback: An adverb of place tells where something happens (here, there, outside, nearby).
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Names an adjective or a noun as the adverb of the sentence.

example.question: Find the adverb: "The old man walked slowly."

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "old" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: An adverb tells about the verb. Slowly tells how he walked.
misconceptions.feedback: An adverb tells more about a verb. In this sentence slowly tells how the man walked. Old describes the man, so it is an adjective.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Calls a word that tells how an adverb of place, because it comes after the verb.

example.question: In "He answered politely", what does politely tell us.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "where" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Politely tells how he answered.
misconceptions.feedback: An adverb of manner tells how an action is done: politely, loudly, carefully, quickly.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Uses good as an adverb (She sings good).

example.question: Achieng sings very ___.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "good" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Good describes a noun. Well describes how someone does something.
misconceptions.feedback: Good is an adjective (a good singer). Well is the adverb (she sings well).
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Adds -ly to fast, hard or late (fastly, lately for late).

example.question: The matatu was going very ___.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "fastly" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Fast is both an adjective and an adverb.
misconceptions.feedback: Fast, hard and late are adverbs without -ly: He ran fast. She worked hard. Lately means recently.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Uses hardly for hard (She studies hardly).

example.question: Njoroge studied ___ for the examination.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "hardly" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Hardly means almost not at all. Hard means with a lot of effort.
misconceptions.feedback: Hard means with great effort. Hardly means almost not: He hardly slept means he slept very little.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Uses an adjective after an action verb (He spoke quiet, she walks slow).

example.question: The teacher spoke ___ to the class.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "quiet" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: An action verb is described by an adverb.
misconceptions.feedback: To tell how an action is done, use an adverb (quietly), not the adjective (quiet).
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Spells the -ly form wrongly (happyly, easyly, truely).

example.question: The boy answered the question ___. (easy)

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "easyly" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: After a consonant, y changes to i before -ly.
misconceptions.feedback: Adjectives that end in y change y to i before -ly: easy, easily; happy, happily.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

learning_experiences: mention words that are difficult to spell correctly,

skills.name: Spell commonly misspelt words
skills.mastery: Spells words that often go wrong (because, friend, believe, beautiful, address, definitely, parliament, necessary, calendar, February) and picks the correct spelling from three that look alike, in 8 of 10 new items.

prerequisites.reason: Grade 6 English taught it first. Proposed, to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

leads_to.reason: Grade 8 English builds on this skill. Proposed, to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

misconceptions.error: Mixes up ie and ei (beleive, freind, recieve).

example.question: My best ___ lives in Kisii.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "freind" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Friend has i before e: fri-end.
misconceptions.feedback: Remember: friend (fri + end), believe (be + lie + ve). After c it is ei: receive.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Doubles or fails to double a letter (adress, neccessary, begining).

example.question: Write your home ___ on the form.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "adress" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Address has two d and two s.
misconceptions.feedback: Some words have double letters: address, necessary (one c, two s), beginning, tomorrow (one m, two r).
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Leaves out a silent letter (Febuary, goverment, libary).

example.question: The class was born in ___.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Febuary" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Say it slowly: Feb-ru-ary has an r in the middle.
misconceptions.feedback: Some letters are not clearly said but must be written: February, government (the n), library (two r).
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Spells a word as it sounds (becuase, definately, beutiful).

example.question: I stayed home ___ I was sick.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "becuase" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Break it up: be-cause.
misconceptions.feedback: Do not spell by sound alone. Because is be + cause. Beautiful is beau + ti + ful. Definitely has finite in the middle.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Writes a sound-alike word with the wrong spelling (alot, wich, wensday).

example.question: Our class meets on ___.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Wensday" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Wednesday has a d that is not said.
misconceptions.feedback: Wednesday has a d that is not said. A lot is two words. Which has a h in the middle.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

sub_strands.sub_strand: Listening Comprehension: Listening for Details (Theme 7: Natural resources – forests)

collaborate with peers to compare the notes, then revise and display for review.

skills.name: Read a table, a chart or a map for information
skills.mastery: Says what kind of information a table, a bar graph, a pie chart, a map, a diagram and a timeline give, and reads a fact from a small table or chart, and does not read a row for a column, in 8 of 10 new items.
question_forms: choose the visual for the need

prerequisites.reason: Grade 6 English taught it first. Proposed, to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

leads_to.reason: Grade 8 English builds on this skill. Proposed, to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

misconceptions.error: Chooses the wrong visual for the information needed (a map to compare amounts).

example.question: Which visual best compares the number of learners in four classes.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "a map" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: A bar graph compares amounts.
misconceptions.feedback: A bar graph compares amounts, a pie chart shows parts of a whole, a map shows places, a timeline shows order in time and a table lists facts in rows and columns.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Reads the wrong row or column of a table.

example.question: Read the table. How many mangoes did Achieng sell on Tuesday.
example.correct_answer: the number in the Tuesday column for Achieng

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "the number for Monday" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Find the row for the person and the column for the day.
misconceptions.feedback: To read a table find the row for the item and the column for the heading, then read where they meet.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Gives a total when one part is asked, or one part when the total is asked.

example.question: Read the table. How many mangoes in all did Achieng sell.
example.correct_answer: the sum of all the days

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "one day only" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Add the days.
misconceptions.feedback: Read the question: one part needs one cell, the total needs all the cells added.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Does not read the title or the key before the data.

example.question: What should you read first in a chart.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "the smallest number" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: The title says what the chart is about.
misconceptions.feedback: Read the title, the headings and the key first. They tell what the figures mean.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

skills.name: Use personal pronouns: I and me, he and him, we and us
skills.mastery: Uses the subject form (I, he, she, we, they) before a verb and the object form (me, him, her, us, them) after a verb or preposition, and does not write me and him went or between you and I, in 8 of 10 new items.

prerequisites.reason: Grade 5 English taught it first. Proposed, to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

skills.name: Use possessive pronouns and possessive adjectives: mine, my, its
skills.mastery: Tells a possessive adjective before a noun (my book) from a possessive pronoun that stands alone (the book is mine), writes its (belonging) and it's (it is) correctly, and does not write her's or your's, in 8 of 10 new items.

prerequisites.reason: Grade 5 English taught it first. Proposed, to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.
This skill builds on it. Proposed, to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

misconceptions.error: Uses the object form as the subject (Me and Juma went; Him is tall).

example.question: ___ and Juma went to the river.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Me" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Before a verb, the subject form is used: I went.
misconceptions.feedback: The subject of a sentence takes I, he, she, we or they. Me, him, her, us and them are for after a verb or preposition.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Uses the subject form as the object (Give the book to I; she saw he).

example.question: The teacher gave the prize to Atieno and ___.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "I" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: After to and other prepositions, the object form is used: to me.
misconceptions.feedback: After a verb or a preposition use the object form: me, him, her, us, them. So: to Atieno and me.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Uses us as a subject or we as an object (Us are going; give it to we).

example.question: The headteacher thanked ___ for the clean compound.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "we" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Thanked needs an object: us.
misconceptions.feedback: We is the subject form (We cleaned). Us is the object form (She thanked us).
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Uses the wrong pronoun for number or gender (the girls ... he, the tree ... she).

example.question: Wanjiru has a younger brother. ___ is in Grade 3.

misconceptions.cause: In Kiswahili one pronoun serves he and she.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "She" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: The brother is a boy, so he.
misconceptions.feedback: A pronoun replaces the noun, so it must fit it: a boy is he, a girl is she, more than one is they and a thing is it.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Repeats the subject with a pronoun (My mother she is a nurse).

example.question: Which sentence is correct.
example.wrong_answer: My mother she is a nurse.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "My mother she is a nurse." next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Name the person once. The noun is the subject, so no pronoun is added.
misconceptions.feedback: Do not add a pronoun after the noun that is already the subject: My mother is a nurse.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Writes it's for belonging, or its for it is.

example.question: The dog wagged ___ tail.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "it's" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: It's means it is. Belonging has no apostrophe: its tail.
misconceptions.feedback: Its (no apostrophe) shows belonging: its tail. It's is short for it is or it has.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Writes her's, your's, their's or our's.

example.question: This book is ___.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "her's" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Possessive pronouns never take an apostrophe.
misconceptions.feedback: Hers, yours, ours, theirs and its never have an apostrophe.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Uses mine before a noun or my where nothing follows (This is my. That is mine book).

example.question: Is this your pencil? Yes, it is ___.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "my" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: When no noun follows, use mine.
misconceptions.feedback: My, your, his, her, our and their come before a noun (my book). Mine, yours, his, hers, ours and theirs stand alone (the book is mine).
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Uses a subject pronoun to show belonging (Me book, he bag, they teacher).

example.question: The boys left ___ bags in the classroom.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "they" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Belonging before a noun uses their.
misconceptions.feedback: To show who owns something, use a possessive: my, your, his, her, its, our, their.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Mixes up their, there and they're.

example.question: The girls took ___ lunch to the field.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.

skills.name: Put the steps of the writing process in order
skills.mastery: Names the steps (planning, drafting, revising, editing, publishing), says what is done at each and puts them in order, and does not edit before the draft is written, in 8 of 10 new items.

misconceptions.error: Puts editing before drafting.

example.question: What do you do first when you write a composition.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "edit it" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: You cannot edit what you have not written. Planning comes first.
misconceptions.feedback: The steps are: planning, drafting, revising, editing, publishing. Planning comes first because you need ideas before you write.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Mixes up revising and editing.

example.question: At which step do you check spelling and punctuation.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "revising" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Revising changes ideas and order. Editing corrects spelling and punctuation.
misconceptions.feedback: Revising is to improve the ideas, the order and the choice of words. Editing is to correct spelling, punctuation and grammar.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Thinks the first draft is the final copy.

example.question: What is a first draft.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "the final clean copy" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: A draft is a first try.
misconceptions.feedback: A first draft is a rough first version written to get ideas down. It is improved later.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Puts publishing in the middle.

example.question: Which step comes last.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "planning" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Publishing is sharing the finished work.
misconceptions.feedback: Publishing comes last: the finished piece is copied neatly and shared.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

skills.name: Use simple prepositions of time, place and direction
skills.mastery: Says whether a preposition shows time (at, on, in), place (beside, under) or direction (to, into, across), chooses at, on or in for times and places, and does not write at Monday or in the morning of Friday, in 8 of 10 new items.

prerequisites.reason: Grade 6 English taught it first. Proposed, to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.
Grade 5 English taught it first. Proposed, to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

misconceptions.error: Chooses the wrong one of at, on and in for a time (at Monday, in 5 o'clock).

example.question: The meeting starts ___ Monday.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "at" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: On for days, at for clock times, in for months and years.
misconceptions.feedback: Use on with days and dates (on Monday), at with clock times and points (at five o'clock) and in with months, years and parts of the day (in March, in the morning).
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Uses to where in is needed, or in where to is needed (She is going in school, he is to Nairobi).

example.question: We are going ___ the market.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "in" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: To shows the direction of movement.
misconceptions.feedback: To shows a movement towards a place (go to the market). In shows where something already is (in the market).
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Names a preposition of place as one of time or direction.

example.question: In "The cat is under the table", what does under tell us.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "time" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Under tells where the cat is.
misconceptions.feedback: A preposition of place shows where something is (under, beside, behind, between). A preposition of direction shows movement (to, into, across).
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Uses on where at is needed for a place (on the bus stop, in the gate).

example.question: Please wait for me ___ the bus stop.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "on" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: At is for a point or a place we wait at.
misconceptions.feedback: At shows a point or a place where something happens (at the bus stop, at the gate, at school). On shows a surface (on the table).
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

skills.name: Choose words by the vowel sounds /ʊ/ and /uː/
skills.mastery: Picks the word with the short sound of put (/ʊ/) or the long sound of food (/uː/), and does not match words by spelling (look and food both have oo), in 8 of 10 new items.
question_forms: pick the word with the same sound

prerequisites.reason: Grade 6 English taught it first. Proposed, to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

misconceptions.error: Judges the vowel sound by the spelling (look and food both have oo).

example.question: Which word has the same vowel sound as "put" (/ʊ/).

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "food" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Say the words aloud. Put and look have the short sound.
misconceptions.feedback: Spelling does not show the sound. Put and look have the short /ʊ/. Food and pool have the long /uː/.
misconceptions.source: to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher: sound judgements depend on the accent the class is taught in

misconceptions.error: Mixes the short /ʊ/ and the long /uː/ sound.

example.question: Which word has the long vowel sound of "pool" (/uː/).

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "pull" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: The /uː/ sound is longer: pool, room, moon, fruit.
misconceptions.feedback: The long /uː/ is in pool, room, food, fruit and moon. The short /ʊ/ is in pull, put, look, book and good.
misconceptions.source: to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher: sound judgements depend on the accent the class is taught in

misconceptions.error: Cannot find the word with a different vowel sound.

example.question: Which word has a different vowel sound: book, good, moon, foot.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "book" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Say each word. Three have the short sound.
misconceptions.feedback: Book, good and foot have the short /ʊ/. Moon has the long /uː/, so it is the odd one out.
misconceptions.source: to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher: sound judgements depend on the accent the class is taught in

misconceptions.error: Uses and where but is needed (She is small and strong).

example.question: Njeri is small ___ very strong.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "and" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: But shows that the two ideas do not go together as expected.
misconceptions.feedback: But joins ideas that contrast. And simply adds. Small is expected to go with weak, so but fits.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Uses or where and is needed, or and where or is needed.

example.question: Would you like tea ___ coffee?

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "and" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: A choice is joined by or.
misconceptions.feedback: Or joins choices (tea or coffee). And joins things that go together (tea and bread).
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Uses two joining words together (But and, and but, or but).

example.question: He was tired ___ he finished the work.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "but and" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: One joining word is enough between two parts.
misconceptions.feedback: Use only one joining word between two parts of a sentence. But and and, or but and or together are wrong.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Joins two sentences with only a comma (It was late, we went home).

example.question: Which sentence is correct.
example.wrong_answer: It was late, we went home.
example.correct_answer: It was late, so we went home.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "It was late, we went home." next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: A comma alone cannot join two sentences; add a joining word.
misconceptions.feedback: A comma alone cannot join two complete sentences. Add a joining word (and, but, so) or start a new sentence.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

example.question: Which list shows the events in the order they happened.

misconceptions.reveals: Offer "two events swapped" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.

misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

example.question: Which list shows the events in the order they happened.

skills.name: Know the features of a narrative composition

This skill builds on it. Proposed, to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

example.correct_answer: On Saturday Achieng lost her purse in the market and had to find it.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "The market is wide, noisy and full of colour." next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.

misconceptions.reveals: Offer "a title" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.

misconceptions.feedback: A narrative needs a problem or a conflict, events and an ending.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

example.question: What is the setting of a story.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "the people in the story" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.

misconceptions.error: Takes an occasion that does not need a speech.

example.question: At which of these would a speech most likely be given.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "a private chat with a friend" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: A speech is for an audience at an occasion.
misconceptions.feedback: Speeches are given at occasions with an audience: a school assembly, a prize-giving, a wedding or a funeral.

misconceptions.error: Puts the parts of a speech in the wrong order (thanks first).

example.question: Which part of a speech comes first.

misconceptions.reveals: Offer "the thanks" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.

misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

example.correct_answer: a note with only what the text says
