skills.name: Use the articles a, an and the
skills.mastery: Chooses a before a consonant sound (a university), an before a vowel sound (an hour, an egg), and the for one named or known thing, and does not use a before a vowel sound or the before a general idea, in 8 of 10 new items.

misconceptions.error: Chooses a or an by the letter, not the sound (an university, a hour).

example.question: Our teacher stayed for ___ hour after school.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "a" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Say the word: hour starts with a vowel sound, so an.
misconceptions.feedback: Choose an before a vowel sound (an hour, an egg, an umbrella) and a before a consonant sound (a university, a uniform, a house).
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Uses a before a vowel (a apple, a orange).

example.question: She ate ___ orange after lunch.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "a" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Orange starts with a vowel sound, so an.
misconceptions.feedback: Use an before a word that starts with a vowel sound: an apple, an orange, an elephant.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Uses the before a general idea or plural (The life is hard; I like the mangoes).

example.question: We should protect ___ environment.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "a" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: The environment around us is one known thing, so the.
misconceptions.feedback: Use the for one particular or known thing (the sun, the environment). Use a or an for one of many.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Leaves out a, an or the where one is needed (She is teacher).

example.question: My aunt is ___ nurse at the hospital.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "no word" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: A job needs a: a nurse.
misconceptions.feedback: A singular noun that can be counted needs a, an or the before it: She is a nurse.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

example.question: A boy found a purse. ___ boy gave it to the teacher.

misconceptions.reveals: Offer "A" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: The boy is the one already mentioned.
misconceptions.feedback: Use a or an the first time (a boy). Use the when the same thing is mentioned again (the boy).
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Uses a word that does not go with one thing (many, these) where a, an or the is needed.

misconceptions.reveals: Offer "many" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: A single thing needs a, an or the.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.

skills.name: Form adjectives from nouns and verbs
skills.mastery: Forms the adjective from a noun or verb with -ful, -less, -y, -ous, -al, -ive or -able (care, careful; danger, dangerous; create, creative), and keeps the spelling right (beauty, beautiful), in 8 of 10 new items.

prerequisites.reason: Grade 6 English taught it first. Proposed, to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.
Grade 6 English taught it first. Proposed, to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

misconceptions.error: Uses the noun where the adjective is needed (a danger road, a beauty girl).

example.question: It is a ___ road at night.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "danger" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Before a noun, an adjective is needed: dangerous.
misconceptions.feedback: An adjective describes a noun. The adjective of danger is dangerous. We do not say a danger road.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Adds the wrong ending (carely, helpness, hopeable).

example.question: The nurse was very ___ with the baby. (care)

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "carely" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Careful means full of care.
misconceptions.feedback: Add -ful for full of (careful, helpful) and -less for without (careless, hopeless). The ending must fit the word.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Keeps the spelling of the noun (beautyful, easyer, fameous).

example.question: The young girl was very ___.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "beautyful" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Y changes to i before -ful: beauty, beautiful.
misconceptions.feedback: The spelling changes: beauty becomes beautiful (y to i), fame becomes famous (the e drops), mud becomes muddy (the d doubles).
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Mixes up -ful and -less (a harmful medicine used for a harmless one).

example.question: The old knife is ___ because it cannot cut. (use)

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "useful" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Cannot cut means without use: useless.
misconceptions.feedback: -Ful means full of (useful, hopeful) and -less means without (useless, hopeless).
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

recognise a closing formula as a feature of dilemma narratives
relate the lessons learnt in the dilemma narrative to real life experiences

skills.name: Know a dilemma narrative and its closing formula
skills.mastery: Says that a dilemma narrative ends with a hard choice put to the listener (Who was right? What would you have done?), picks the closing question, and tells it from a narrative that ends with a lesson, in 8 of 10 new items.

prerequisites.reason: Grade 6 English taught it first. Proposed, to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

misconceptions.error: Thinks a dilemma narrative ends with a lesson told by the narrator.

example.question: How does a dilemma narrative end.
example.wrong_answer: with the narrator telling the lesson
example.correct_answer: with a hard question to the listener

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "with the narrator telling the lesson" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: A dilemma leaves the choice to the listeners.
misconceptions.feedback: A dilemma narrative ends with a question that leaves the listeners to decide: Who was right?
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Picks a question that is not a closing formula.

example.question: Which is a closing formula of a dilemma narrative.
example.correct_answer: Who do you think was right?

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "What time is it?" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: It asks the listener to choose.
misconceptions.feedback: The closing formula puts the dilemma to the audience, for example Who was right? What would you have done?
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Thinks any story with two characters is a dilemma.

example.question: Which story is a dilemma narrative.
example.wrong_answer: a story with an easy ending
example.correct_answer: a story where both choices are hard

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "a story with an easy ending" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: A dilemma has two hard choices.
misconceptions.feedback: A dilemma narrative puts a character or the listener before a hard choice where each side has a good reason.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

skills.name: Choose and spell synonyms and antonyms
skills.mastery: Chooses and writes a word with the same meaning (synonym) or the opposite meaning (antonym) in a sentence, spells it correctly, and does not give a word that is related but not the same, in 8 of 10 new items.

prerequisites.reason: Grade 6 English taught it first. Proposed, to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.
Grade 6 English leads to this outcome. Proposed, to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

skills.name: Write numbers in words and spell them correctly
skills.mastery: Spells numbers in words (fourteen, forty, ninety, eighth), writes ordinals with the right ending (1st, 2nd, 3rd, 4th, 21st) and puts the hyphen in twenty-one to ninety-nine, in 8 of 10 new items.

prerequisites.reason: Grade 6 English taught it first. Proposed, to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.
Grade 6 English taught it first. Proposed, to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.
Grade 6 English leads to this outcome. Proposed, to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

misconceptions.error: Gives a related word instead of a synonym (big for huge is right, but big for building is not).

example.question: Which word means the same as "tiny".

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "small" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: A synonym can replace the word.
misconceptions.feedback: A synonym has almost the same meaning and can replace the word in the sentence.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Gives a synonym when an antonym is asked, or the other way round.

example.question: Which word is the opposite of "ancient".

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "old" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: An antonym has the opposite meaning.
misconceptions.feedback: A synonym means the same. An antonym means the opposite: ancient and modern are antonyms; ancient and old are synonyms.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Makes an antonym only by adding un- or not (unhot, not-big).

example.question: The opposite of "generous" is ___.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "ungenerous" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Not every antonym is made with un-.
misconceptions.feedback: Many antonyms are different words (generous, selfish). Do not make an opposite by adding un- to every word.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Chooses a synonym that does not fit the sentence.

example.question: Which word can replace "bright" in "She is a bright pupil".

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "shiny" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: A word can have more than one meaning. Check which meaning fits the sentence.
misconceptions.feedback: A word may have different synonyms for different meanings. In this sentence bright means clever, not shiny.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Spells forty as fourty or fourteen as forteen.

example.question: Write 40 in words.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "fourty" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Forty has no u, but four and fourteen have.
misconceptions.feedback: Four and fourteen have a u. Forty has no u. Ninety has an e before ty.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Writes an ordinal with the wrong ending (1th, 2th, 3th, twenty-oneth).

example.question: Our school sports day is on the 22___ of May.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "22th" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Numbers ending in 2 take nd.
misconceptions.feedback: Ordinals: 1st, 2nd, 3rd, then th (4th to 20th), then 21st, 22nd, 23rd, 24th.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Leaves out the hyphen in twenty-one to ninety-nine.

example.question: Write 45 in words.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "forty five" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Join the two words with a hyphen.
misconceptions.feedback: Numbers from twenty-one to ninety-nine are written with a hyphen: twenty-one, forty-five.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Spells the ordinal wrongly (eigth, nineth, twelvth).

example.question: He finished in ___ place.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "eigth" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Eighth has two h, one in eigh and one in th.
misconceptions.feedback: Spell the ordinal in words: eighth (eight + h), ninth (no e), twelfth (twelve loses the e and adds fth).
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Begins a sentence with a figure (40 learners came).

example.question: Which sentence is correct.
example.correct_answer: Forty learners came to the meeting.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "40 learners came to the meeting." next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Never begin a sentence with a figure.
misconceptions.feedback: A sentence must not begin with a figure. Write the number in words: Forty learners came.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Spells a number word wrongly (ninty, fourty, forteen).

example.question: Write 90 in words.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "ninty" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Ninety has an e before ty.
misconceptions.feedback: Say the number slowly and spell each part: nine + ty = ninety (the e stays), four + teen = fourteen, but forty has no u.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

sub_strands.sub_strand: Listening: Views/ Opinions (Theme 12: Traditional fashion)

listen to an oral narrative and identify the different ways used to express opinions/views,

sub_strands.core_competences:
Learning to learn: It is enhanced as learner searches online and offline for the different ways of expressing views and opinions.
Digital literacy: It is enhanced as the learner interacts using technology when searching online and listening to an oral narrative from digital gadgets.

Respect is enhanced as the learner appreciates diverse opinions as they conduct the role play.

skills.name: Use expressions that give a view or an opinion
skills.mastery: Chooses the expression that shows a view (In my opinion, I believe, I feel that, As I see it), tells a view from a fact, and agrees or disagrees politely (I see your point, but ...), in 8 of 10 new items.

prerequisites.reason: Grade 6 English taught it first. Proposed, to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

leads_to.reason: Grade 8 English builds on this skill. Proposed, to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

misconceptions.error: Takes a fact for an opinion, or an opinion for a fact.

example.question: Which sentence gives an opinion.
example.correct_answer: In my opinion, football is the best sport.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Kenya has 47 counties." next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: An opinion shows what someone thinks or feels.
misconceptions.feedback: A fact can be checked. An opinion says what a person thinks or feels, often with words such as in my opinion, I believe or best.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Chooses a phrase that does not show a view (First, finally, however).

example.question: Which expression shows your view.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "First of all" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: These words say what you think.
misconceptions.feedback: Expressions that show a view are in my opinion, I believe that, I feel that and as I see it.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Disagrees rudely (That is wrong, you know nothing).

example.question: Which is a polite way to disagree.
example.correct_answer: I see your point, but I think differently.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "That is nonsense." next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Respect the other person while you disagree.
misconceptions.feedback: Disagree politely: I see your point, but ... or I respectfully disagree.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Gives a view with no reason.

example.question: Which gives a view with a reason.
example.wrong_answer: I think school uniform is bad.
example.correct_answer: I think school uniform is good because it makes all learners look equal.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "I think school uniform is bad." next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Give a reason after the view.
misconceptions.feedback: A good view is supported by a reason, often with because.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

skills.name: Use phrasal verbs with put, come and give
skills.mastery: Gives the meaning of put on, put off, put out, come across, come up with, give up, give in and give away from the sentence, and picks the right particle, not a word that only looks like it, in 8 of 10 new items.

prerequisites.reason: Grade 6 English taught it first. Proposed, to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

leads_to.reason: Grade 8 English builds on this skill. Proposed, to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.
Grade 8 English builds on this skill. Proposed, to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

misconceptions.error: Mixes up put off, put out and put on.

example.question: The firefighters ___ the fire in the market.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "put off" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Put out means to stop a fire. Put off means to delay.
misconceptions.feedback: Put out means to stop a fire or a light. Put off means to delay. Put on means to wear.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Mixes up give up, give in and give away.

example.question: The thief refused to ___ and run away.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "give away" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Give up means to stop trying. Give away means to give for free.
misconceptions.feedback: Give up means to stop trying. Give in means to agree after refusing. Give away means to give something for free.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Reads the phrasal verb word for word (come across means to cross).

example.question: While cleaning, Ouma ___ an old photograph.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "came out" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Come across means to find by chance.
misconceptions.feedback: Come across means to find or meet by chance. Come up with means to think of. The meaning is not the sum of the words.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Uses the wrong little word (come out with an idea for come up with an idea).

example.question: The class tried to ___ a good name for the club.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "come out with" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Come up with means to think of something.
misconceptions.feedback: Come up with an idea, a plan or a name means to think of one. The particle cannot be changed.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Reads put on as put something on top (put on a jacket as place a jacket).

example.question: It was cold, so Baraka ___ his jacket.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "put out" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Put on means to wear.
misconceptions.feedback: Put on means to wear or to switch on. Put out means to stop a fire.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

skills.name: Know the format of a written dialogue
skills.mastery: Puts the speaker's name, a colon and the words spoken on a new line for each turn, writes actions in brackets, and does not use quotation marks round every line of a play-style dialogue, in 8 of 10 new items.
question_forms: find the mistake in a dialogue

prerequisites.reason: Grade 6 English taught it first. Proposed, to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

leads_to.reason: Grade 8 English builds on this skill. Proposed, to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

misconceptions.error: Writes a play-style dialogue with quotation marks round every line.

example.question: Which is the correct play-style dialogue.
example.correct_answer:
Atieno: Good morning.
Juma: Good morning.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer ""Atieno: Good morning." "Juma: Good morning."" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: In a script the speaker name and a colon show who is speaking.
misconceptions.feedback: In a written dialogue (a script) the speaker's name and a colon begin each line. Quotation marks are for direct speech inside a story.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Runs the speakers together on one line.

example.question: How should each speaker's words be written.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "on the same line" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Each turn starts on a new line.
misconceptions.feedback: Each speaker's turn begins on a new line, so the reader sees who is speaking.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Writes actions without brackets so they look like spoken words.

example.question: How are actions such as smiling shown in a dialogue.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "in quotation marks" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Brackets show it is not spoken.
misconceptions.feedback: Actions and feelings are written in brackets after the speaker's name, for example Atieno (smiling): Good morning.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Leaves out the speaker's name.

example.question: What does each line of a dialogue start with.
example.correct_answer: the speaker's name and a colon

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "the words spoken" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Without a name we do not know who speaks.
misconceptions.feedback: Each line begins with the name of the speaker and a colon, then what the person says.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

skills.name: Use words about land travel
skills.mastery: Chooses the right word (passenger, fare, route, junction, conductor, terminus, luggage, timetable, journey, destination) to complete a sentence about travel, and does not mix a person with a place or a thing, in 8 of 10 new items.

prerequisites.reason: Grade 6 English taught it first. Proposed, to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

misconceptions.error: Mixes a person and a place (conductor and terminus).

example.question: The matatu ___ collected the fares.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "terminus" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: The person who collects fares is the conductor.
misconceptions.feedback: A conductor is the person who collects fares. A terminus is the place where a route ends.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Uses fare where another word is needed (school fare, bus fee).

example.question: The ___ from Nakuru to Eldoret is 400 shillings.

misconceptions.cause: Fee and fare are both used for payment.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "fee" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: A fare is the money paid for a journey.
misconceptions.feedback: A fare is the money paid for a journey. A fee is paid for a service such as school.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Mixes journey, route and destination.

example.question: Kisumu is our final ___.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "route" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: The place you are going to is the destination.
misconceptions.feedback: The journey is the travelling. The route is the way taken. The destination is the place you are going to.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Writes luggages or baggages.

example.question: The passengers put their ___ on the roof of the bus.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "luggages" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Luggage is not counted.
misconceptions.feedback: Luggage and baggage have no plural. Say luggage or pieces of luggage.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Mixes timetable with ticket or route.

example.question: The bus ___ shows when each bus leaves.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "ticket" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: A timetable lists times.
misconceptions.feedback: A timetable lists the times when buses or trains leave. A ticket is proof that you have paid the fare.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

This skill builds on it. Proposed, to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

misconceptions.error: Chooses one detail as the main idea.

example.question: What is the main idea of the passage.
example.correct_answer: what the whole passage is about

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "a detail from one paragraph" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: The main idea covers the whole passage.
misconceptions.feedback: The main idea is what the whole passage is about. A detail is one fact in it.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Chooses an idea that is much wider than the passage.

example.question: What is the main idea of the passage.
example.correct_answer: a statement of the passage's own topic

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "a very wide statement" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: The main idea must fit this passage.
misconceptions.feedback: A main idea must fit the passage. If it is much wider, it is not the main idea of this passage.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Chooses an idea that is not in the passage.

example.question: What is the main idea of the passage.
example.wrong_answer: an idea that is not in the passage

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "an idea that is not in the passage" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Check that the passage says it.
misconceptions.feedback: The main idea must be in the passage.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Gives a detail near the one asked for.

example.question: What was the thing the question asked for.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "a nearby detail" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Read the question word.
misconceptions.feedback: A detail question asks for one exact fact. Find the line with the key word of the question.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Gives one detail as the summary.

example.question: Which is the best summary of the passage.
example.correct_answer: the key ideas in a few lines

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "one detail" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: A summary covers the whole passage.
misconceptions.feedback: A summary covers all the key ideas in a few words. A single detail is not a summary.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Chooses the opening lines copied as the summary.

example.question: Which is the best summary of the passage.
example.correct_answer: a short account of the whole passage

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "the first lines copied" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: A summary is in your own words.
misconceptions.feedback: A summary is in your own short words and covers the whole passage, not only the opening.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Adds something the passage does not say.

example.question: Which is the best summary of the passage.
example.wrong_answer: a summary with a new idea
example.correct_answer: a summary with only the passage's ideas

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "a summary with a new idea" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: A summary adds nothing new.
misconceptions.feedback: A summary keeps only the ideas of the passage and adds nothing new.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Gets the order of the key ideas wrong.

example.question: Which summary keeps the ideas in the right order.
example.wrong_answer: the ideas in a mixed order
example.correct_answer: the ideas in the passage's order

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "the ideas in a mixed order" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Keep the order of the passage.
misconceptions.feedback: A summary keeps the key ideas in the order of the passage.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Picks a line that only gives a fact as the one that paints a picture.

example.question: Which line paints a picture.
example.wrong_answer: a line that states a fact
example.correct_answer: a line with sights, sounds or movement

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "a line that states a fact" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: A picture line uses the senses.
misconceptions.feedback: A line that paints a picture uses sights, sounds, smells or movement. A line that only states a fact does not.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Chooses a picture that the words do not make.

example.question: What does this line help you to see.
example.wrong_answer: something the line does not show

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "something the line does not show" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Use all the words in the line.
misconceptions.feedback: Use all the words together to see the picture, not only one word.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Reads a picture word for word (the clouds were wool as real wool).

example.question: What does the line mean.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "a word-for-word meaning" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: The writer compares to help you picture.
misconceptions.feedback: A writer compares things to help the reader picture them. The comparison is not meant word for word.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Chooses a meaning from a word that looks like the hard word.

example.question: What does the word mean in the passage.
example.wrong_answer: a meaning from a similar-looking word

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "a meaning from a similar-looking word" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Use the sentence, not the look of the word.
misconceptions.feedback: Do not guess from how a word looks. Use the words around it.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Uses the common meaning of a word that has another meaning here.

example.question: What does the word mean in the passage.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "its common meaning" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Try the meaning in the sentence.
misconceptions.feedback: A word may have more than one meaning. Choose the one that fits the sentence.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Chooses the opposite meaning.

example.question: What does the word mean in the passage.
example.correct_answer: the same meaning as the clues show

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "the opposite meaning" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Check the words around it.
misconceptions.feedback: The clues in the passage show what the word means. Check you have not chosen the opposite.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Picks words that are not a clue to the hard word.

example.question: Which words in the passage help you understand the word.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "words unrelated to the word" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: A clue explains or describes the word.
misconceptions.feedback: A clue is a group of words near the hard word that tells more about it.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Gives a detail that is near the answer but is not the answer.

example.question: Which answer is stated in the passage.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "a nearby detail" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Match the question word.
misconceptions.feedback: The answer is written in the passage. A detail beside it may answer a different question.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Uses outside knowledge that the passage does not give.

example.question: Which answer is stated in the passage.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "something from your own knowledge" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Use only the passage.
misconceptions.feedback: A factual question is answered from the passage, not from what you already know.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Says a stated fact is false or not stated.

example.question: Is it true, false or not stated.
example.wrong_answer: False or Not stated for a stated fact

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "False or Not stated for a stated fact" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Find the sentence that says it.
misconceptions.feedback: If the passage says it in so many words, it is true.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Says a false statement is true.

example.question: Is it true, false or not stated.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "True for a false statement" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: The passage says the opposite.
misconceptions.feedback: If the passage says something different, the statement is false.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Says a false statement is not stated.

example.question: Is it true, false or not stated.
example.wrong_answer: Not stated for a false statement

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Not stated for a false statement" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: The passage does speak about it, and says something different.
misconceptions.feedback: If the passage speaks about it and says something different, the statement is false, not "not stated".
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Says a statement the passage does not mention is true or false.

example.question: Is it true, false or not stated.
example.wrong_answer: True or False for a statement not in the passage

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "True or False for a statement not in the passage" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: The passage does not say.
misconceptions.feedback: If the passage does not say, the answer is not stated, even if the statement sounds likely.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Goes beyond the clues in the passage.

example.question: Which can you work out from the passage.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "a claim with no clue" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: An inference needs a clue.
misconceptions.feedback: An inference must be supported by clues in the passage.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Gives an answer that goes against the passage.

example.question: Which can you work out from the passage.
example.wrong_answer: a claim the passage goes against
example.correct_answer: a claim that fits the passage

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "a claim the passage goes against" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Check the answer against the passage.
misconceptions.feedback: An inference must agree with what the passage says.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Copies a stated sentence as an inference.

example.question: Which can you work out from the passage, though it is not written.
example.wrong_answer: a sentence copied from the passage
example.correct_answer: something worked out from the clues

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "a sentence copied from the passage" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: An inference is not written; it is worked out.
misconceptions.feedback: A sentence copied from the passage is stated, not worked out. An inference is worked out from clues.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

skills.name: Tell a simple sentence from a fragment and write one
skills.mastery: Says that a simple sentence has one subject and one verb and tells a complete thought, tells it from a fragment that has no verb or no subject, and from two sentences joined without a joining word, in 8 of 10 new items.

prerequisites.reason: This skill builds on it. Proposed, to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.
Grade 6 English taught it first. Proposed, to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

leads_to.reason: Grade 8 English builds on this skill. Proposed, to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

misconceptions.error: Takes a group of words with no verb or no subject for a sentence (The tall girl from Kisumu).

example.question: Which is a complete simple sentence.
example.correct_answer: The tall girl comes from Kisumu.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "The tall girl from Kisumu." next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: A sentence needs a subject and a verb and a complete thought.
misconceptions.feedback: A simple sentence needs a subject and a verb and tells a complete thought. A group of words with no verb is a fragment.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Calls a sentence with and, but or so a simple sentence.

example.question: Which is a simple sentence.
example.wrong_answer: Kamau ran fast, but he lost the race.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Kamau ran fast, but he lost the race." next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: A simple sentence has one subject and one verb idea.
misconceptions.feedback: A simple sentence has one main clause. A sentence joined with and, but or so has two and is a compound sentence.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

example.question: Which is a complete simple sentence.

misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Red apples and ripe mangoes." next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.

misconceptions.error: Gives a wrong purpose for a praise song (to insult, to teach arithmetic).

example.question: What is the main purpose of a praise song.
example.correct_answer: to honour a person for what he or she has done

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "to insult a person" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: A praise song honours someone.
misconceptions.feedback: A praise song honours a person, such as a chief, a champion or a bride, and tells of what makes the person special.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Mixes up the singer and the one praised.

example.question: Who is praised in a praise song for the winner of a race.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "the singer" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: The singer praises someone else.
misconceptions.feedback: The singer (or praise poet) honours another person. The one praised is the subject of the song.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Thinks praise songs must be exactly true to the last detail.

example.question: Why does a praise song say the runner is faster than the wind.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "because it is a fact" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Exaggeration shows admiration.
misconceptions.feedback: Praise songs use exaggeration (hyperbole) and praise names to show great admiration.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Names an occasion that does not suit a praise song.

example.question: At which occasion is a praise song most likely sung.
example.correct_answer: at a wedding or a victory celebration

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "at a quarrel" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Praise songs are for occasions of honour.
misconceptions.feedback: Praise songs are sung at ceremonies and celebrations such as weddings, victories and installations.

create well-written narrative compositions using the specified idioms
appreciate the role of idioms in creative writing

skills.name: Explain the meaning of idioms in context

prerequisites.reason: Grade 6 English taught it first. Proposed, to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

leads_to.reason: Grade 8 English builds on this skill. Proposed, to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

misconceptions.error: Reads an idiom word for word (it is raining cats and dogs means animals fall).

example.question: What does "it is raining cats and dogs" mean.
example.wrong_answer: animals are falling from the sky

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "animals are falling from the sky" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: An idiom means more than its words.
misconceptions.feedback: An idiom has a meaning that is not the same as its words: raining cats and dogs means raining very hard.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Gives a meaning that fits one word of the idiom but not all.

example.question: What does "spill the beans" mean.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "to cook a meal" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Think of what happens when beans spill.
misconceptions.feedback: Spill the beans means to tell a secret by mistake.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Changes a word in the idiom (a piece of pie, hit the nail on the finger).

example.question: Complete: It was a piece of ___. (very easy)

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "pie" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: The words of an idiom are fixed.
misconceptions.feedback: An idiom cannot be changed: a piece of cake, not a piece of pie.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

sub_strands.sub_strand: Consonant Sounds and Intonation (Theme 14: Sports - outdoor games)
learning_experiences: search from print and non-print sources for tongue twisters with some of the target sounds and say them for enjoyment,

watch a video or listen to a recording or conversation on outdoor games and group the words in a table according to the following target sounds: v/ as in very; /f/ as in ferry /n/ as in been an /ŋ/ as in being,
listen to, and model native speaker clips with the target sounds in words,
work with peers to practise the pronunciation of words with the target sounds and record themselves,

outcomes.text: identify words with the sounds /v/, /f/, /n/ and /ŋ/ from a text

use correct intonation for yes/no and wh-questions in varied contexts
appreciate the importance of correct pronunciation and intonation in a conversation

skills.name: Choose words by the consonant sounds /t/, /d/, /l/, /r/, /v/, /f/, /n/ and /ŋ/
skills.mastery: Picks the word that starts or ends with the sound named, tells /f/ from /v/ (five, fiver) and /n/ from /ŋ/ (sin, sing), and does not match by spelling, in 8 of 10 new items.
question_forms: pick the word with the same sound

prerequisites.reason: Grade 6 English taught it first. Proposed, to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

misconceptions.error: Mixes the sounds /f/ and /v/ (fan and van sound the same).

example.question: Which word starts with the sound /v/.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "fan" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Touch your throat: /v/ shakes, /f/ does not.
misconceptions.feedback: /f/ is a quiet sound (fan, five). /v/ is voiced, you feel it in your throat (van, vine).
misconceptions.source: to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher: sound judgements depend on the accent the class is taught in

misconceptions.error: Mixes the final sounds /n/ and /ŋ/ (sin and sing).

example.question: Which word ends with the sound /ŋ/.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "sin" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Sing ends with the sound at the back of the mouth.
misconceptions.feedback: /ŋ/ is the ending of sing, long and ring. /n/ is the ending of sin, fun and ran. There is no separate g sound in sing.
misconceptions.source: to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher: sound judgements depend on the accent the class is taught in

misconceptions.error: Mixes the sounds /l/ and /r/ (light and right sound the same).

example.question: Which word starts with the sound /r/.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "light" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: For /l/ the tongue touches the top; for /r/ it does not.
misconceptions.feedback: /l/ and /r/ are different sounds. Light starts with /l/, right starts with /r/.
misconceptions.source: to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher: sound judgements depend on the accent the class is taught in

misconceptions.error: Mixes the sounds /t/ and /d/ (tin and din).

example.question: Which word starts with the sound /d/.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "tin" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: /d/ is voiced, /t/ is not.
misconceptions.feedback: /t/ is not voiced (tin, ten). /d/ is voiced (din, den).
misconceptions.source: to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher: sound judgements depend on the accent the class is taught in

misconceptions.error: Matches by the letter instead of the sound.

example.question: Which word ends with the sound /f/.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "of" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Say each word. Of ends in /v/. Laugh ends in /f/.
misconceptions.feedback: The sound is not always the same as the letter: laugh ends in /f/ but of ends in /v/.
misconceptions.source: to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher: sound judgements depend on the accent the class is taught in

skills.name: Find the subject and the verb and make them agree
skills.mastery: Finds the subject and the verb of a sentence, makes the verb agree with a singular or plural subject (The boys play, the boy plays), and does not let a noun near the verb decide the agreement (The box of mangoes is heavy), in 8 of 10 new items.

prerequisites.reason: This skill builds on it. Proposed, to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

misconceptions.error: Makes the verb agree with the noun beside it, not the subject (The box of mangoes are heavy).

example.question: The basket of mangoes ___ heavy.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "are" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: The subject is the basket, one thing.
misconceptions.feedback: The verb agrees with the subject (the basket), not the noun near it (mangoes). So: The basket of mangoes is heavy.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Uses a singular verb with a plural subject (The boys plays).

example.question: The boys ___ in the field.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "plays" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: More than one boy takes the plain verb.
misconceptions.feedback: A plural subject takes a plural verb: The boys play. The girls were.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Uses a plural verb with a singular subject (My sister like music).

example.question: My sister ___ music.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "like" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: One sister takes likes.
misconceptions.feedback: A singular subject takes the singular verb: My sister likes. The teacher has.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Uses a singular verb after two subjects joined by and (Juma and Otieno is friends).

example.question: Juma and Otieno ___ good friends.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "is" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Two people joined by and take are.
misconceptions.feedback: Two subjects joined by and are plural, so the verb is plural: Juma and Otieno are.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Names the verb or the object as the subject.

example.question: What is the subject of "The farmer sells vegetables"

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "sells" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: The subject is who or what does the action.
misconceptions.feedback: The subject is who or what does the action. The verb is the action itself.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Uses a plural verb with everyone, each or nobody (Everyone are ready).

example.question: Everyone ___ ready for the trip.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "are" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Everyone means every one person, so is.
misconceptions.feedback: Everyone, everybody, each, nobody and someone take a singular verb: Everyone is ready.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Uses there is with a plural noun (There is three books on the table).

example.question: There ___ four chairs in the room.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "is" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Four chairs is plural, so are.
misconceptions.feedback: After there the verb agrees with the noun that follows: there is a chair, there are four chairs.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

skills.name: Find dialogue, similes and metaphors in a text and use them
skills.mastery: Says that dialogue is the words characters speak, a simile compares with like or as and a metaphor says one thing is another, picks each from a short text, and completes a simile or a metaphor, in 8 of 10 new items.

prerequisites.reason: Grade 6 English taught it first. Proposed, to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.
Grade 6 English taught it first. Proposed, to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

leads_to.reason: Grade 8 English builds on this skill. Proposed, to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

misconceptions.error: Calls a simile a metaphor or a metaphor a simile.

example.question: Which is a metaphor.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "He ran like the wind." next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: A simile uses like or as.
misconceptions.feedback: A simile compares with like or as. A metaphor says one thing is another.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Does not see which part of a text is dialogue.

example.question: Which sentence is dialogue.
example.wrong_answer: The sun rose over the hill.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "The sun rose over the hill." next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Dialogue is what the characters say.
misconceptions.feedback: Dialogue is the words characters say to each other, usually in quotation marks.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Writes as ... like or like ... as in a simile.

example.question: Complete: as brave ___ a lion.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "like" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: The pattern is as ... as.
misconceptions.feedback: A simile uses as ... as or like: as brave as a lion, or brave like a lion.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Reads a metaphor as true (the classroom was a zoo).

example.question: In "the classroom was a zoo", what does the writer mean.
example.correct_answer: the class was noisy and wild

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "there were animals in it" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: A metaphor does not mean the words literally.

misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

skills.name: Know the features of descriptive writing
skills.mastery: Names what makes writing descriptive (the five senses, adjectives and adverbs, similes, an order such as top to bottom), tells a description from a narrative, and picks the sentence with the best detail, in 8 of 10 new items.

prerequisites.reason: This skill builds on it. Proposed, to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.
Grade 6 English taught it first. Proposed, to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

leads_to.reason: Grade 8 English builds on this skill. Proposed, to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

misconceptions.error: Takes a story of events for a description.

example.question: Which text is descriptive writing.
example.wrong_answer: We walked to the lake and then swam.
example.correct_answer: The lake was calm and silver, and the air smelled of wet grass.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "We walked to the lake and then swam." next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: A description shows what something looks, sounds or feels like.
misconceptions.feedback: Descriptive writing paints a picture of a person, a place or a thing, using the senses. A narrative tells events.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Thinks listing facts is a description.

example.question: Which sentence is the best description.
example.wrong_answer: The market opens at six o'clock.
example.correct_answer: The market bursts with the smell of fresh bread and the shouts of sellers.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "The market opens at six o'clock." next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: A description uses the senses: see, hear, smell, touch, taste.
misconceptions.feedback: A good description uses the senses and exact words, not only facts.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Describes in a jumbled order.

example.question: In what order is a building usually described.
example.correct_answer: in a clear order, such as from the front to the back

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "in any order" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: A reader must follow where you are looking.
misconceptions.feedback: A description follows a clear order, such as top to bottom, near to far or front to back.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Uses vague words such as nice and good instead of exact ones.

example.question: Which sentence has the best detail.
example.correct_answer: The ugali was hot and soft, with a smoke-sweet smell.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "The food was nice." next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Exact words let the reader picture it.
misconceptions.feedback: Use exact words (hot, soft, smoky) instead of vague words such as nice, good or very.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

sub_strands.sub_strand: Oral Reports (Theme 15: Tourist attraction sites - kenya)
learning_experiences: brainstorm the content and organisation of an oral report e.g. introduction, body, and conclusion,
search online and offline in pairs, the steps for conducting an oral report e.g. research, compile (write), rehearse, and report (present/deliver),
role-play methods of delivering oral reports such as clear pronunciation, voice projection, tonal variation, use of non-verbal cues, and use of visuals,
use flashcards to prepare speaking notes for the reports,
simulate an oral report preparation and delivery procedure and video or audio record themselves,
watch or listen to the recorded reports and evaluate them in terms of strengths and weaknesses,
collaborate with peers to prepare and present actual oral reports,
write the reports on charts and share them with peers for evaluation,
key_inquiry_questions: How can you make an oral report presentation interesting?
sub_strands.core_competences:

sub_strands.pcis: Effective communication is enhanced as learners use verbal and non-verbal reporting skills.

outcomes.text: outline the organisation of an oral report of events within the classroom
present an oral report on events that occur within the classroom
enjoy delivering and listening to oral reports in various contexts

skills.name: Know how an oral report of an event is organised
skills.mastery: Puts the parts of an oral report in order (greeting, what happened, who, when and where, the end), and picks the sentence that opens or closes a report, in 8 of 10 new items.

prerequisites.reason: Grade 6 English taught it first. Proposed, to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

leads_to.reason: Grade 8 English builds on this skill. Proposed, to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

misconceptions.error: Puts the parts of an oral report in the wrong order.

example.question: Which part of an oral report comes first.
example.correct_answer: a greeting and what the report is about

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "the end of the event" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Start by saying what you will report.
misconceptions.feedback: An oral report begins with a greeting and what it is about, then tells what happened, who, when and where, and ends with a closing.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Adds one's own opinion where only the facts are wanted.

example.question: Which sentence belongs in an oral report on a fire drill.
example.correct_answer: The drill began at ten o'clock and the whole school reached the field in four minutes.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "The drill was so boring." next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: A report tells what happened.
misconceptions.feedback: A report gives the facts: what happened, who, when, where. Personal opinions are left out.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Ends a report without a closing.

example.question: Which sentence best closes an oral report.
example.wrong_answer: And then the bell rang and
example.correct_answer: That was the end of the event. Thank you for listening.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "And then the bell rang and" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: A closing tells the report is complete.
misconceptions.feedback: An oral report closes with a short ending and thanks: That is my report. Thank you for listening.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Reports a past event in the present tense.

example.question: Which sentence is correct in a report on yesterday's match.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "The team win the match." next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: An event that has finished is reported in the past.
misconceptions.feedback: A report on an event that has finished uses the past tense: The team won the match.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

sub_strands.sub_strand: Reading Fluency (Theme 15: Tourist attraction sites - kenya)
learning_experiences: watch and listen to videos of students reading fluently and discuss what makes them good readers,

search online and offline for different reading fluency strategies such as previewing and predicting, skimming, scanning, and ignoring unknown words and share with peers, watch or listen to sample reading clips and simulate the model reading as they apply reading strategies,
practise, with peers, timed reading, accurate reading, and reading with expression on issues like tourist attraction sites in Kenya,
assess peers’ reading based on the aspects of fluency – accuracy, speed, reading,
record sample readers in class and save the recordings on a digital device,

Effective Communication is enhanced as the learner develops competence in fluency as a reading skill.
Environmental Education is enhanced as the learner reads about tourist attraction sites in Kenya.

apply fluency strategies while reading

skills.name: Recognise the strategies of reading fluently
skills.mastery: Names how a fluent reader reads (the right speed, a changing voice for feelings, a short pause at a comma and a longer one at a full stop, words read in groups, a text read again) and tells a fluent reader from one who reads flat, too fast or word by word, in 8 of 10 new items.

leads_to.reason: Grade 8 English builds on this skill. Proposed, to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

misconceptions.error: Thinks a fluent reader reads in one even voice with no feeling.

example.question: Which helps you to read with expression.
example.wrong_answer: reading every word in the same flat voice
example.correct_answer: changing your voice to show feelings and pausing at full stops

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "reading every word in the same flat voice" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Expression means the voice shows the meaning.
misconceptions.feedback: A fluent reader changes the voice to show feelings, and pauses at commas and full stops.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Thinks fluent reading is reading as fast as possible.

example.question: Which is reading at the right speed.
example.correct_answer: not too fast and not too slow, so the listener can follow

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "as fast as possible" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Fluent reading can be understood.
misconceptions.feedback: The right speed is steady, so that the listener can follow. Reading too fast loses the meaning.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Reads one word at a time and stops at every hard word.

example.question: Which is a way to read more fluently.
example.correct_answer: reading the same short text several times

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "stopping at every difficult word" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Fluent reading flows in groups of words.
misconceptions.feedback: A fluent reader reads words in groups and reads a text again to make it smooth. Stopping at every word breaks the flow.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

sub_strands.sub_strand: Affirmative and Negative Sentences (Theme 15: Tourist attraction sites - kenya)
learning_experiences: search online and offline for the differences between affirmative and negative sentences and share them with peers,
role-play a dialogue with affirmative and negative sentences and record themselves,
watch/listen to a conversation on issues like tourist sites in Kenya and pick out the affirmative and negative sentences,
sort jumbled up sentences into affirmative and negative sentences,
construct affirmative and negative sentences,
share sentences made in the form of charts for peer review,
write a short story or dialogue on an issue like tourist attraction sites in Kenya using affirmative and negative sentences.
key_inquiry_questions: When do we use affirmative statements?
When do we use negative statements?
Why is it important to use the right sentence when saying something?
sub_strands.core_competences:
Citizenship: It is enhanced in using critical inquiry as learners make affirmative and negative sentences on the tourist attraction sites in Kenya.
Digital literacy: It is developed as learner uses digital devices to search online and offline for the differences between affirmative and negative sentences and shares them with peers.

Unity is enhanced as learners share sentences made in the form of charts for peer review.
Patriotism is enhanced as the learner nurtures love for own country by reading texts on tourist attraction sites.
sub_strands.pcis:
Citizenship Education is enhanced through texts on tourist sites in Kenya.
Creative Thinking is enhanced as learners create dialogue and stories using declarative sentences.
sub_strands.links: The learner relates the concept of affirmative and negative sentences to their learning of language use in Kiswahili.

outcomes.text: differentiate between affirmative and negative sentences in spoken and written contexts
construct affirmative and negative sentences in varied contexts
acknowledge the expressive role of sentences in effective communication

skills.name: Write affirmative and negative sentences
skills.mastery: Tells an affirmative sentence from a negative one, makes a sentence negative with do not, does not, did not, is not or cannot, and does not write a double negative (I do not have no pen), in 8 of 10 new items.

prerequisites.reason: This skill builds on it. Proposed, to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.
This skill builds on it. Proposed, to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.
Grade 6 English taught it first. Proposed, to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

misconceptions.error: Uses two negatives (I do not have no pen).

example.question: I do not have ___ pen.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "no" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: One negative is enough: do not have a pen, or have no pen.
misconceptions.feedback: Use only one negative word. Say I do not have a pen, or I have no pen.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Uses don't after he, she or it (She don't like beans).

example.question: She ___ like beans.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "don't" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: One person takes does not.
misconceptions.feedback: After he, she, it or one name use does not or doesn't: She doesn't like beans.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Uses did not with the past form (She did not went).

example.question: He did not ___ to school yesterday.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "went" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: After did not the plain verb is used.
misconceptions.feedback: After did not use the plain verb: She did not go. Did already shows the past.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Puts not in the wrong place (I am go not).

example.question: Which sentence is negative and correct.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "She not is here." next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Not follows is, are, was, were, can, will, or do/does/did.
misconceptions.feedback: Not comes after the helping verb: is not, can not (cannot), will not, does not.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Uses no where not is needed, or not where no is needed (I am no tired).

example.question: I am ___ tired.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "no" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Not goes with a verb or an adjective. No goes with a noun.
misconceptions.feedback: Use not to make a verb or adjective negative (I am not tired). Use no before a noun (I have no time).
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Calls a negative sentence affirmative, or the other way, when no not appears (Nobody came).

example.question: Which sentence is negative.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Everybody came." next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Nobody means not anybody.
misconceptions.feedback: A sentence is negative if it says that something did not happen. Nobody, nothing, never and none make a sentence negative even without not.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

sub_strands.sub_strand: Poetry (Theme 15: Tourist attraction sites - kenya)
learning_experiences: collaborate with peers to recite poems for enjoyment and outline the subject matter,
search online and offline for ways of determining ideas in a poem, such as studying the title, the persona, the events, and the choice of words,
discuss how the use of repetition and other styles can help bring out the ideas in the poem,
collaborate with peers to pick a poem and identify the ideas brought out and share their findings with peers through charts or graphic organisers for review,
dramatise a poem displaying ideas generated from it using placards and record their performances.
key_inquiry_questions: Why would you use a poem instead of a story to pass information?
What makes a poem interesting to read?
What kind of ideas can one convey using a poem?
sub_strands.core_competences:
Problem Solving: It is enhanced when finding extra information as learners search online and offline for ways of determining ideas in a poem.
